Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 20

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as we pointed out last week, most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time.
  • Photo: Ludovic Laude/L’Est Republicain.
  • A normally timid mountain ungulate has been attacking runners on the outskirts of Besançon in eastern France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as we pointed out last week, most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents that have come to light recently.

Chamois in France. Photo: Ludovic Laude/L’Est Republicain.

A normally timid mountain ungulate has been attacking runners on the outskirts of Besançon in eastern France.

In a recent development, one victim, a 30-year-old woman jogger, was knocked unconscious and suffered a punctured shoulder and serious scalp wounds requiring stitches and staples. The incident occurred just a few hundred meters from the outskirts of the city.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t hear it coming,” the woman, known only as Milena, told Le Monde. “I only had time to see its head 10 centimeters from me, and then, nothing, total blackout…”.

The woman was unconscious for about five minutes.

Industry observers note that another runner had been attacked days earlier. The incidents occurred near La Chapelle des Buis. Wildlife authorities described the behavior as highly unusual and authorized the animal’s removal. The cause of its aggression remains unclear.

A 71-year-old Winter Garden, Florida fisherman, Steven Hamilton, was posing for a photograph with a fish when a large alligator lunged from the water, seized his leg, and pulled him into a pond.

Emergency crews responded, but the alligator refused to let go of his body, according to Fox News. By the time they released him and killed the alligator, Hamilton was dead. The medical examiner identified drowning and blunt-force injury to his left leg as causes of death, with alligator tooth marks on both sides of the leg.

In a recent development, alligator attacks are rare but occur occasionally. According to the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, there have been a total of 500 alligator bites against humans since 1948, including 32 fatal encounters.

Asiatic black bear. Photo: Shutterstock.

Vladimir Odulo, a fisherman from Primorye in Russia’s Far East, survived an attack by an Asiatic black bear, also known as a Himalayan bear.

According to recent reports, the bear attacked while Odulo was fishing. He tried to defend himself with his fishing rod, but the animal knocked him into the water. Odulo continued fighting as it “beat his face like a boxer,” Russian media reported the fisherman saying. Suddenly, the bear stopped the attack and fled into the forest.

Odulo suffered several wounds and a serious eye injury, but survived. Doctors in Vladivostok were able to save his eyesight.

Sources indicate that A venomous Caspian cobra, which now occurs high in Himachal Pradesh. Photo: Shutterstock.

According to recent reports, two deaths in the Indian Himalaya have been attributed to Caspian cobras. Native to Central Asia, this venomous species has expanded its range eastward into the higher reaches of Himachal Pradesh. It now also occurs in Pakistan and Kashmir.

The first death occurred when a 40-year-old man accidentally stepped on a Caspian cobra while spraying an apple orchard. Wearing open-toed footwear, he sustained two bites on his leg. He was taken to a local faith healer before being shifted to the hospital, where he was declared dead, according to the Tribune of India.

In the second case, a 62-year-old man stepped on a snake while on his way to work and was bitten on the leg. He collapsed within half an hour and was taken to a health facility, where he died.

Recent findings suggest that these fatalities occurred some time ago, but the report on them was published just this week in the journal Epidemiology International. The Caspian cobra generally inhabits higher, open, rocky terrain at elevations of 2,000m or higher, where both incidents occurred. Researchers suggest its range may now include lower elevations.

It has been revealed that A charging elephant. Photo: Shutterstock.

Two men died in separate elephant attacks in northern Kenya.

Recent findings suggest that on October 11, Eisimgai Gorow Ltarakwa, 41, was herding goats near Nguposorogin village when a lone elephant attacked him. He suffered severe injuries and died at the scene.

Two days later, Mukhtar Abdoy Hussein, 64, was grazing livestock near Benane village when a herd of elephants trampled him to death.

It has been revealed that the incident highlights the risks faced by herders in areas where livestock grazing activities bring communities into close proximity with wildlife. Under a conservation initiative, the families are entitled to receive compensation, according to Kenyan media.

A 76-Year-Old Kazakh Blacksmith Is Walking Around the World

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, sarsenbay Kotyrashov had never left his native Kazakhstan when, in 2023, he set out to walk across the Caucasus.
  • Sources indicate that now, three years later, Kotyrashov has almost 30,000 followers on Instagram who have tuned in for his journeys on foot across Eurasia.
  • In a recent development, alongside his growing social media presence, Kotyrashov has been working with UNESCO to document Kazakh artisanal practices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sarsenbay Kotyrashov had never left his native Kazakhstan when, in 2023, he set out to walk across the Caucasus. A blacksmith from the industrial province of Ulytau in central Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov had in tow only a battered suitcase and his signature leather hat as he crossed the Kazakh border. He was 73 years old.

Sources indicate that now, three years later, Kotyrashov has almost 30,000 followers on Instagram who have tuned in for his journeys on foot across Eurasia. People stop him and ask for selfies with Ulytauman, his online moniker and a reference to his home province.

In a recent development, alongside his growing social media presence, Kotyrashov has been working with UNESCO to document Kazakh artisanal practices. He is now 76, and his travels are far from over.

In a recent development, kotyrashov started his first job at age nine, working as a herder. By the time he entered his 70s, he had worked an astonishing diversity of manual labor jobs: carpenter, joiner, stonemason, lathe operator, metalworker, and most recently blacksmith. His expertise in traditional artisanship landed him a job at the Ulytau National Reserve Museum, a 150,000-hectare open-air museum comprising everything from mountains to mausoleums. From 2010 to 2020, Kotyrashov worked restoring historical buildings on the reserve, some of which date back to the Bronze Age.

Recent findings suggest that the mausoleum of Jochi Khan, a 12th century Mongol ruler, is only one of the 25 building complexes at the Ulytau National Museum Reserve. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

Industry observers note that tourists came from around the world to visit the reserve. Kotyrashov began to dream of traveling like them. “Why not?” he asked himself. “Why haven’t I seen the whole world myself? In my entire life, I’ve only ever seen Ulytau and Astana.”.

It has been revealed that then came the pandemic, and his wife of 40 years passed away. Kotyrashov built a small hand-cart and set out across Kazakhstan on foot. “I chose to travel on foot, because when you walk, you notice much more, including nature, landscapes, animals, and plants,” he explained. “There is also time to think, to reflect, and to understand things.”.

Kotyrashov’s first journey in 2022 was a love letter to Kazakhstan. As he walked from town to town over 181 days, pulling a homemade cart weighing around 60kg, he spoke with local artisans about their crafts. He tied a flag to his cart to promote the Qymyzmuryndyk festival, which celebrates the traditional Kazakh drink of kumis, or fermented mare’s milk. Local governments began holding press conferences for him and organizing lodging.

Photo: Sarsenbay Kotyrashov/Instagram.

In a recent development, “Each day, I would meet with anywhere from 150 to 500 people in different parts of the country,” he told a Kazakh outlet. “The greatest discovery of my journey was the people — the citizens of Kazakhstan. They are generous, kind, noble, and open-hearted; I was truly struck by the kind of people who inhabit our Kazakhstan. It gives me hope for a better future.”.

In 2023, he crossed the border into Russia, then followed the spine of the Caucasus Mountains through Chechnya and Georgia, and finally into Türkiye. Sometimes, he bivouacked in his sleeping bag. In towns, though, Chechen and Ingush Georgian locals invited him to stay with them. In Türkiye, he slept in mosques.

In a recent development, kotyrashov decorated his cart with flags celebrating Kazakhstan. Photo: Kazinform.

It has been revealed that after his trip to Türkiye, Kotyrashov tackled China. Unlike in Central Asia and the Caucasus, he finally had to pay for hotels. By now, though, he had secured a trip coordinator and sponsors who helped him cover the costs. He took photos at the Great Wall and ended his journey in Beijing.

Europe posed greater difficulties. Everywhere else he had visited, he walked along the side of the highway. Unbeknownst to him when he began his 2026 trip, 3,000km from Belgrade to Paris, walking on highways is largely illegal in Europe. He had replaced his cart with an old suitcase, but the suitcase bit the dust on an unpaved footpath 150km outside Paris.

But Kotyrashov had an appointment. Determined to make it, he left the suitcase behind and sped on with his backpack.

It has been revealed that on April 24th, he arrived at the UNESCO World Heritage Center in Paris and presented officials there with a handmade iron bell. At the Center, he met with Kazakhstan’s permanent UNESCO representative and shared his research on Kazakh artisanship and nomadic travel.

Recent findings suggest that kotyrashov on the Great Wall of China. Photo: Astana Times.

Recent findings suggest that after returning from Paris, Kotyrashov began working once more as a blacksmith to save up for his next trip. Sponsors help him with lodging and food, but he still needs to pay for his own gear. “Over the course of six months, I wore out seven pairs of shoes,” he mentioned.

In 2027, he will set out to another continent: the Americas. He aims to cross the United States from coast to coast, starting in Florida and ending in California. After his experience in Europe, he’s studying up on American highway law.

Recent findings suggest that three years ago, Kotyrashov left Kazakhstan for the first time. Now, he’s hoping the American trip will contribute to his broader goal of claiming a Guinness record for the most miles walked by a person over 75.

“I had never traveled far in my life,” he stated. “But it is never too late to travel.”.

Photo: Sarsenbay Kotyrashov/Instagram.

Year          Route                                                                                   Distance.

2022      Across Kazakhstan, ending in Aktau on the Caspian Sea       ~8,000km.

2023     Atyrau, Kazakhstan → Russia → Caucasus → Türkiye             ~3,000km.

2024     Kazakhstan → Russian Altai → Mongolia → China                   uncertain.

2026    Belgrade → Hungary → Austria → Germany → Paris                 ~3,000km.

In a recent development, open a CreditStrong account if your credit history is short or damaged and you can make every payment on autopay, since it reports to all three credit bureaus without checking your credit. Its Instal loan adds up to $349 in interest and fees over 48 months, so price a credit union’s credit-builder loan first.

CreditStrong, a division of Austin Capital Bank, sells two credit-builder loans, Instal and MAGNUM, that lock the money you borrow in savings until you’ve repaid it, plus Revolv, a credit line sold by subscription. Instal, the entry loan, releases $1,010 after 48 monthly payments, and by our math its interest and fees add up to $349.

Recent findings suggest that creditStrong suits borrowers with a short or damaged credit history who can keep each payment on autopay for the full term. Borrowers who can join a credit union should price its credit-builder loan first, and anyone who might miss a payment is safer with Revolv’s yearly blueprint, which requires no monthly payment.

Amelia Earhart Search Find Trees, Not Plane. Mystery Remains

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University recently returned from Nikumaroro, a remote and uninhabited atoll in the Pacific Ocean.
  • According to recent reports, their primary objective was to investigate the Taraia Object, a mysterious shape in a shallow lagoon that researchers first noticed in 2020 on satellite and historical aerial photos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A highly anticipated expedition to solve one of aviation’s greatest mysteries has concluded without finding the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s missing plane.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University recently returned from Nikumaroro, a remote and uninhabited atoll in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, their primary objective was to investigate the Taraia Object, a mysterious shape in a shallow lagoon that researchers first noticed in 2020 on satellite and historical aerial photos. While some hoped the anomaly was the remnants of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra, the expedition determined it was entirely natural.

Industry observers note that the Taraia Object on a satellite image. Located at Nikumaroro. Photo: Archaeological Legacy Institute.

According to Purdue University officials, the object was a cluster of large fallen trees resting on a sandbar. Much of the debris observed in satellite images had already broken up and washed away, leaving a single Y-shaped piece. The reflective, metallic glint seen from above turned out to be a hardened layer of coral sand coating the wood.

On the way to the atoll. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

The five-day operation proved logistically complicated. Workers faced dense brush and a large population of giant coconut crabs. The nocturnal activities of the massive crabs forced the crew to abandon plans to camp on the atoll and to return to the ship each evening. During the day, the crabs simply minded their own business.

One of the crew holds a coconut crab. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

Despite the difficulties, researchers recovered a few minor artifacts to study lagoon drift patterns, including a 76cm steel tube.

The team emphasized that ruling out the Taraia Object does not disprove the broader “castaway hypothesis.” For decades, historians have investigated the theory that Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan drifted off course during their 1937 global circumnavigation attempt, landing on Nikumaroro’s reef after failing to find Howland Island.

Amelia Earhart. Photo: amelia.prf.org.

Purdue University, where Earhart once served as a career counselor and aviation advisor, stated that its commitment to the search remains unchanged.

In a recent development, “Amelia Earhart never gave up — she kept pushing boundaries and flying into the unknown,” mentioned Steve Schultz, Purdue’s general counsel and field assistant, after the expedition. “She kept flying, and we will keep searching.”.

For more details, extensive project documentation, and a gallery of expedition photographs, you can visit the official mission site at Amelia.prf.org.

It has been revealed that from left to right: Steve Schultz, Sirisha Bandla, and Marc Hagle, members of the research team. Photo: Purdue Research Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jost Kobusch is back in Nepal, preparing for the fourth round of his Everest project. His long-term goal is to climb solo in winter, without oxygen, self-supported, and via the Lho La and the West Ridge.

“If I am good at something, it’s planning,” the 34-year-old German told ExplorersWeb. In this case, his plan is to arrive at the mountain in the best shape possible, physically and mentally.

Kobusch arrived in Kathmandu two weeks ago, together with friends Nicolas Scheidtweiler, Manuela Brummer, and photographer Alex Pichon. The group soon moved to Manang in the Annapurna region and began acclimatizing in the Chulu range.

Sources indicate that jost Kobusch (in yellow) scouts around Manang. Photo: Alex Pichon.

Sources indicate that the plan was to spend a few nights at altitude and traverse the four Chulu peaks, all above 6,000m. “[However,] expeditions rarely unfold exactly as expected,” Kobusch admitted.

It has been revealed that A member in the team felt exhausted after reaching the summit of the second peak, and the group abandoned the traverse there. “At least, we traversed from the summit of Chulu Far East (6,059m) to the top of Chulu East (6,444m) from the southeast,” Kobusch said. He indicates their line between the two peaks was upcoming.

In a recent development, the line followed by Kobusch and his team up Chulu East. Photo: Alex Pichon.

Industry observers note that their next plan will be to climb a 7,000m peak in the area before Kobusch moves to the Khumbu in November. “I want to reach 8,000m, but on a different mountain than Everest, before the beginning of winter,” he said.

Sources indicate that he wants to be completely acclimatized by the time he starts working on Everest on December 22, the start of calendar winter. Kobusch will have two photographers in Base Camp, but he will climb alone.

Acclimatization in Manang, Photo: Alex Pichon.

Industry observers note that “I need to be able to move efficiently, make good decisions when I’m tired, manage risk alone, and stay comfortable in an environment where very small mistakes can have very serious consequences,” Kobusch recently wrote on social media. He says that so far, all is going well. “I’m feeling good, I’ve done my homework, and I will start again on Everest better prepared than ever.”.

Kobusch has attempted winter Everest solo on three previous occasions, always via the Lho La and the West Ridge, thus avoiding venturing alone into the Khumbu Icefall.

In a recent development, in his first attempt in 2019-20, he reached the West Shoulder and pushed above 7,300m. On the second attempt in 2021-22, high winds didn’t let him go beyond 6,400m. He planned to try again the following year, but he caught dengue fever while training in Nepal and had to cancel.

Once recovered, he soloed Denali in February-March 2023. Everest had to wait one more year, this time due to a back injury. On the third attempt in 2024-25, he reached his highest point yet: 7,537m on December 27.

Kobusch’s highest point is shown with a green circle, and the Hornbein Couloir is the pink line on the 3D map by RealityMaps.

“The chances of success are not particularly high,” he recently wrote. “If I had to put a number on it, I would say around 20%. But that does not make the attempt meaningless. If anything, it is part of what makes it interesting.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most important things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who at the moment draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

In a recent development, but for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

In a recent development, those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an important subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

Sources indicate that but when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

That little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

It has been revealed that in between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

Sources indicate that first let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

When you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

It has been revealed that at that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

Sources indicate that it means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be massive enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

In a recent development, if you’re newly introduced to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

What this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

In a recent development, now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:.

Industry observers note that whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result! Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

In a recent development, to really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a substantial lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:.

So the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:.

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

And of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

It has been revealed that the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a significant boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

According to recent reports, yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

Sources indicate that sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Now this is the root of the matter. In fact, worry is the root of almost all challenges. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions.

Industry observers note that to illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35. Look at the difference in their benefits:.

Sources indicate that so the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the major earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

One other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI.

Even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. If you want to learn more, I’ve found the AI tools (Anthropic’s Claude, Google Gemini or OpenAI’s Chat GPT) to be shockingly useful at answering questions and running analyses. If you haven’t started using these in your financial research, I highly recommend them. In a recent development, “The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

According to recent reports, “We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”.

To make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

Industry observers note that “We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like fresh credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

Industry observers note that one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That stated, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Recent findings suggest that some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

Industry observers note that while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Industry observers note that many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

In a recent development, of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an glitch with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

In a recent development, either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#21675. Industry News: Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1190 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1190 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident.
  • Sources indicate that “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada.
  • Industry observers note that from there, it was a slippery slope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

Sources indicate that “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”.

Industry observers note that from there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from New Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

In a recent development, but that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”.

According to recent reports, colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice.

According to recent reports, rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form fresh ones where necessary.

Sources indicate that “I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”.

Unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

In a recent development, as he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

In a recent development, “This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”.

The Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Sources indicate that the route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

In a recent development, “I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” stated Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

Industry observers note that “The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”.

Industry observers note that rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

In a recent development, “For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”.

However, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

According to recent reports, the Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice.

In a recent development, overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is notable because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

“This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”.

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a big project, almost as big as the hike itself.

It has been revealed that “I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the significant challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”.

According to recent reports, the Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Sources indicate that once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”.

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

Recent findings suggest that rice looking down on Island Lake from Ulysses S. Grant Peak. Photo: Donovan Rice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

In a recent development, hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

Industry observers note that the team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Recent findings suggest that several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

Hidesuke Taneishi on the summit of Pholesobi Peak. Photo: Hiroki Yamamoto.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been confirmed.

In a recent development, first, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it says on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

In a recent development, the Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”.

Black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”.

The Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre mentioned.

According to recent reports, pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal.

The Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a fresh perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”.

It has been revealed that cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a new light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

According to recent reports, the Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling important routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”.

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks.
  • In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems.
  • Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it showed Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

In the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

Vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first key Italian treatise on the subject.

In a recent development, vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:.

Sources indicate that “The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”.

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library.

Sella’s most vital Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Recent findings suggest that filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

The peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

Sources indicate that sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

Industry observers note that from other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

Muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

It has been revealed that the French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

The British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

Industry observers note that on July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

Recent findings suggest that muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours.

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly showed the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

It has been revealed that they fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

After the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

In a recent development, far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

Sources indicate that the southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal.

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

Recent findings suggest that in August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal.

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a new route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

It has been revealed that the 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

Muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

According to recent reports, these popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

Sources indicate that on the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

It has been revealed that true Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

In a recent development, one of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

In a recent development, another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

Industry observers note that true Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

Industry observers note that the cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

In a recent development, financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable strategy to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

It has been revealed that one of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

It has been revealed that moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a blueprint that fit my unique situation and goals.

According to recent reports, personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

Industry observers note that for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

It has been revealed that ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive proposal to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most crucial thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This full-length adventure documentary follows kayaker Dane Jackson and a small team down Chile’s remote and wild Rio Cuervo.

With an entire river to descend, the film wastes no time getting right into it. Dane Jackson rolls out into the complicated business of trip logistics, trying to find a way to get the team and their equipment to the beginning of the river. Besides him, the team consists of the trip’s mastermind, Kilian Astorga, and kayakers Tom Dolle, Eirik Hansen, Adrian Mattern, and David Sodomka.

Industry observers note that forty years ago, there was a road up to Lake Mayuin, the volcanic pool from with Rio Cuervo flows. It’s gone now, so they turn to helicopter transport. With their gear dangling below on a rope, the chopper carries them up into the mountain, depositing kayaks and kayakers alike on the lakeshore. They set up camp and settle in to begin the first descent of the Rio Cuervo.

Industry observers note that the team scouts the head of the river, swelled with recent rainfall. Photo: Screenshot.

The dense forest and sometimes steep banks add another layer of difficulty as they begin to make their way downstream. They have to initiative ahead, as there are stretches where it is impossible to bail if the rapids become too much. This means more portaging, which is painfully slow due to the thick vegetation.

In a recent development, when they do hit the rapids, on-board cameras capture the frenetic energy of whitewater kayaking. But the film makes no attempt to conceal the reality of a first descent. Much of their time is spent scouting ahead by drone, poring over satellite images, portaging, and standing about debating logistics.

Recent findings suggest that sunset arrives before the end of their portage. Camping in the jungle makes for an uncomfortable night. Photo: Screenshot.

Jackson and the rest of the crew soldier on, though, cracking nerdy jokes (the jungle is compared to both Dagobah and Fangorn Forest) and making the best of bad weather and rough camping. In the final few days, conditions improve, and they can spend more time on the water.

The contrast between their slow, grueling push forward and the wild speed on the river brings refreshing energy to the kayaking sections. When the river finally widens as they glide into the sea, it feels like a hard-won victory.

Running a 3.5km gorge. Photo: Screenshot.

It has been revealed that early in the production of a certain musical, Broadway director Harold Prince attempted to ask Andrew Lloyd Weber what the deeper political allegory or social commentary was behind the composer’s feline opus. Weber famously took a long pause and replied: “Hal, this is just about cats.”.

Recent findings suggest that this movie is about kayaking. Many outdoor adventure films use the genre, and the adventure story, to explore grand themes, and some do so successfully. But when they fall flat, is it more annoying than I can begin to express. For that reason, I deeply respect the clarity of purpose evinced by Dan Jackson and First Descent Rio Cuervo.

Karl Bushby, shortly after starting and now. Photo Facebook.

By our math, the bonus and its 3.50% rate earn about $90 more on that sum over six months than an account paying 4.40%. Once the bonus posts, move your savings to the higher rate.

Tiered Savings is the higher-paying of Barclays’ two online savings accounts, but its 3.50% annual percentage yield (APY) trails the 4.40% Pibank pays with no minimum balance. Pibank sends money out by wire, which your bank may charge to receive, yet on $50,000 Barclays’ lower rate pays $450 less a year by our math, more than twice the one-time bonus.

Savers with more than $25,000 earn the most by moving just the $25,000 the bonus asks and keeping the rest at a higher rate. Below $25,000 there’s no bonus, and Barclays’ 3.50% earns less from the first day than Pibank’s 4.40%.
