#21557. Latest Update: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Dane Steadman Interview: Hard Going and High Stakes in the Karakoram

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure.
  • According to recent reports, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler.
  • Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there is much more to an expedition than summit or failure. In this exclusive interview, American climber Dane Steadman explains why his recent fresh route on Karakoram’s Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) “was much more difficult than the one on Yashkuk Sar, both on and off the mountain.” Strong words, considering that he and his partners were awarded a Piolet d’Or for Yashkuk Sar.

According to recent reports, the one factor on the team’s side was the previous experience of Steadman and Cody Winckler. “It was our third trip, so we knew a lot more about climbing there,” Steadman stated. Indeed, after Yashkuk Sar, Winckler and Steadman returned to Pakistan in 2025 and climbed two newly introduced routes with Blake Berghoff.

Grant Stewart of Canada, the third member of the Sosbun Brakk team, is a skilled climber but was less familiar with the Karakoram. His most remarkable climbs had taken place in Alaska and at home in the Canadian Rockies.

In a recent development, bivy in an ice cave. Photo Dane Steadman.

Comparing the two epic climbs, Steadman highlighted the differences.

Recent findings suggest that “The trip to Yashkuk Sar went incredibly smoothly. Getting there and acclimatizing was great. We had an amazing weather window for the climb. Nothing on it was exceptionally hard, and we did it on the first try, and the descent went without a hitch,” he remarked.

He explained that the hardest parts of that 2024 first ascent were their lack of experience and the uncertainty that came with it. An unexpected mishap also occurred during the climb itself: a snow mushroom collapsed above them, forcing them to change their ascent route halfway up.

“On the other hand,” Steadman went on, “almost everything about the Sosbun Brakk trip was hard: lost bags, sickness acclimatizing, big storms beforehand and while on the mountain, hard climbing and route-finding, and a very difficult descent through terrible weather.”.

Industry observers note that the unclimbed north face of Sosbun Brakk. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“[Overall,] on the Yashkuk trip, I think we felt for most of the time that we would be able to do it with only some moments of doubt here and there,” Steadman admitted. “On Sosbun, we thought much of the time that we wouldn’t be able to do it for all the reasons above. We were quite surprised [to succeed].”.

According to recent reports, one unusual aspect of the Sosbun Brakk expedition was its dates. They went to Pakistan and climbed in early fall, two months later than the Karakoram’s typical July-August climbing season. Yet, Steadman indicates this was planned to account for the changing climate in the high ranges.

Sources indicate that approaching the face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“First, while the Karakoram doesn’t receive as much of the Indian monsoon as the main Himalaya, it is still a monsoonal climate, and I think (and have heard from many locals now) that the weather tends to be much better in the fall than in the summer,” he explained.

Industry observers note that “Second, we were concerned about rockfall and generally unsafe conditions on the face, being relatively low and lacking in buttresses. We thought the colder temperatures would make things safer and increase the odds of finding good ice.

In a recent development, “Third, Grant was able to get time off in October more easily than earlier in September. In a perfect world, we probably would have gone one to two weeks earlier, but we worked with what we had.”.

Recent findings suggest that asked about other expeditions planning to visit the Pakistani mountains in the future, Steadman suggests that October could be a good time for certain climbs, but that September is also great. “This year, the weather was much less stable in September-October than I’ve experienced on my previous trips. Things got much snowier than normal for that time of year, [according to locals], but I think the weather was still better than through most of the summer.”.

The team planned a single alpine-style push in the purest style. However, when they started on the route, they encountered an impassable hanging serac. They had to retreat and decide whether to try a totally different line or go home.

Recent findings suggest that the base camp crew. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The team decided to try a route to the right of the originally planned one. But how could they be sure they wouldn’t reach another dead end?

Steadman admitted it was difficult. “The line we ended up climbing was entirely hidden from view at our base camp and where we acclimatized,” he explained. “[It was] an east-facing gash on a north face, which we only saw from the northwest until we tried it. From all the views we had before the first attempt, the central line we first attempted appeared to be the only route that wouldn’t involve climbing huge walls of monolithic gneiss, as it followed ice streaks and sheets for a good amount of it, and only looked to have relatively short cruxes.

At the base, they discovered that a tiny but menacing serac hung over the center of the wall, threatening the lower half. (The upper half appeared protected by an overhanging rock wall above it.).

“So we shifted to a different line to the left, which looked much harder but possible, and planned to rejoin our intended line at mid-height, under the protection of the overhangs.

Recent findings suggest that that attempt didn’t so much dead-end as things compounded, forcing a retreat. “We were tired even on the approach from non-stop efforts to get there and acclimatize. We had some equipment challenges, were moving slowly, and most of all, the climbing was damn hard,” he noted.

In a recent development, in the end, they chose to rappel down after a two-hour-plus lead climb on a pitch that hadn’t looked hard from below. Dusk was approaching; there was no bivy spot in sight, and they were only 300m up the 1,800m wall.

Recent findings suggest that “However, from our position on that attempt, we were able to see the right-trending, east-facing gash on the right side of the face, which was totally hidden by monolithic rock walls from all our previous vantage points,” he noted. “So, after bailing, we felt like the central line would require fresh bodies, minds, and a huge weather window, but the right-hand line would be much more feasible.”.

Heading up. Photo: Dane Steadman.

The climbers rested for three days in base camp and then set off again. “We certainly felt that we could get shut down at any number of points, especially at the steep mushroom-choked chimney on the headwall below the junction with the northwest spur,” Steadman admitted. “But it seemed like there was a good chance we could do it, and, most importantly, we felt like we could bail from anywhere [if necessary].”.

According to recent reports, the summit ridge of Sosbun Brakk after many tough decisions. Photo: Dane Steadman.

It has been revealed that however, bailing would not be easy. “The lower part would involve rappelling off V-threads, he explained, and if they had to turn back below the headwall, they would need to rappel out right to an icefield.

Route topo: line of ascent in red, line of descent in yellow. Photo: Steadman/Stewart.

In a recent development, the trio summited on their fifth day on the wall, at 4 pm. Days were now short, and they still had a long, uncertain descent ahead. The descent began on the line of ascent, but eventually deviated to newly introduced terrain.

“We descended the upper half of our route, almost entirely rappelling down the northwest spur, with a little bit of downclimbing/traversing),” Steadman said.

They then reached a point west of their ascent line, where the face was slightly smaller and more covered in permanent ice. “Then we rappelled straight down, diagonaling back left partway down to avoid some serac hazard.”.

Recent findings suggest that descending in worsening weather. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that dane Steadman and Cody Winckler of the U.S., together with Grant Stewart of Canada, completed the first ascent of the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m) in Pakistan’s Karakoram last month. The peak had been climbed only once before, by a Japanese team in 1981, from a different, milder side. The upcoming 1,800m route includes difficulties of M7, WI5.

#21550. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1069 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Sources indicate that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Recent findings suggest that crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an key figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Sources indicate that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up looks for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

Recent findings suggest that as the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

Sources indicate that the caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

According to recent reports, the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

Recent findings suggest that the main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Recent findings suggest that attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

In a recent development, the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and New Mexico.

The few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” says Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

Sources indicate that the columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

Sources indicate that according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

Industry observers note that the arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

Recent findings suggest that there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

It has been revealed that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

“The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Vasiliev noted that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

In a recent development, baia says the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no fresh soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Sources indicate that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

Andrew Skurka on Why Experienced Backpackers Don’t Wear Hiking Boots

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The backpacking equivalent of “happy wife, happy life” is “happy feet, happy hike.” So today, I’m going to help guide your decision-making when selecting footwear for your next backpacking trip.
  • According to recent reports, hi, I’m Andrew Skurka.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The backpacking equivalent of “happy wife, happy life” is “happy feet, happy hike.” So today, I’m going to help guide your decision-making when selecting footwear for your next backpacking trip.

According to recent reports, hi, I’m Andrew Skurka. I’m a former thru-hiker. I was the first person to do the Great Western Loop, the Alaska-Yukon Expedition, and the Sea-to-Sea Route.

If you’re watching this before Saturday, December 5th, 2026, and if you live in the Denver metro area, we’re going to have a great time, and you can get tickets here.

Finally, before we get started, we’re opening applications for our 2027 guided backpacking trips on Monday, December 7th. You can find more information here.

Recent findings suggest that footwear plays an outsized role in your backpacking trip. It’s one of the most key decisions that you’ll make as a backpacker when selecting your equipment, and just honestly, it’s really difficult to enjoy yourself on a backpacking trip if every step hurts or feels uncomfortable.

In a recent development, and it doesn’t help that the industry also uses a lot of technical jargon to describe their shoes. It can be pretty overwhelming if you’re not familiar with how shoes are constructed and the different features of them.

Before we talk about backpacking footwear, I think it would be worth looking at some of the other outdoor sports that we might be familiar with. So, for example, biking or skiing or running.

And if you know a serious skier or a serious biker or a serious runner, you know that they don’t have just one pair of shoes. They have multiple pairs of shoes. And when we talk about not just shoes, but multiple skis, multiple bikes, and when we talk about their collection or their quiver, they’ll say their quiver of skis. Each of those sets of skis, each of those bikes, has a specific application or purpose.

So, as an example, let me just kind of walk you through my little collection of running shoes.

Industry observers note that let me start with my trail running shoe. You’ll notice that the shoe has a narrower foot shape to give me good control laterally when I’m on uneven terrain. It also has an aggressive outsole for good traction on dirt and rocks.

In a recent development, this is what I would consider to be like my bike trail or gravel path trail shoe. The outsole is much less aggressive, and it’s a more comfortable upper. It’s a little bit wider, so I can run in the shoe for more time without feeling like my foot’s being constricted.

It has been revealed that this is my road shoe. This outsole is almost nonexistent, has very little traction, and the big highlight feature about the shoe is all this thick foam so I can run on pavement without breaking my bones.

According to recent reports, and then the last shoe I have with me, this is my racing shoe. This has some fancy, super high-tech foam that has a lot of energy rebound and makes me faster. And then the upper is also very minimalist, very minimally designed, very lightweight, so that it doesn’t slow me down over the course of those 26 miles.

So that’s just one example. These are my running shoes.

If you meet a biker or a skier, they’re gonna have the same thing. A skier’s gonna have their cross-country skis and their skate skis and their alpine skis and alpine touring skis, and then their, you know, you name it.

There’s, I think, what’s the saying? “n+1” is where you should stop buying skis.

And then bikers are gonna be the same way. They have their road bikes, their mountain bikes, their gravel bikes, their townies. Okay, same thing.

Now, interestingly, when we talk about backpacking shoes, there is really no consideration in the industry of what the optimal application is of a backpacking shoe.

Recent findings suggest that if you look at backpackers who are on the cutting edge of backpacking, what you’ll see is that they don’t wear boots. The footwear that they choose isn’t actually designed for backpacking. The footwear that backpackers who are on the cutting edge of backpacking wear, they’re trail runners. They’re not even designed for backpacking. And it just happens to be probably the closest thing that is suitable for our particular activity.

What I want to emphasize to you when you’re looking at shoes, first, is that you want to be looking at what the optimal application of a particular shoe is.

So I’ll walk you through the features of a shoe and talk to you about the different conditions in which those sorts of features excel.

And then the other consideration when you’re buying a shoe is that you need to make sure that it fits you.

So at the end, we’ll talk about fit and how to make sure that it’s not just like the best backpacking shoe of 2026, but it’s the best backpacking shoe for the trip that you’re going on and that fits your foot.

Before we talk about how to pick a shoe for the right conditions, let’s actually talk about the parts of the shoe.

According to recent reports, let’s start with the outsole. This is going to be on the bottom of the shoe. It’s where literally the rubber meets the road.

It is going to be typically made out of some kind of rubber compound. There is a trade-off between sticky rubber and durable rubber. So just be aware of that trade-off when you are looking at shoes.

The other thing to be looking at with your footwear is going to be the lugs, including the lug pattern, the lug depth, and also the lug volume.

Generally speaking, for softer surfaces like mud or sand or snow, you want lugs that are taller and that have shorter edges to them.

Industry observers note that and then the opposite is true, too. If you’re going to be walking on flat benched trails, your lug pattern doesn’t need to be as aggressive.

The next part of the shoe I want to talk about is the midsole. This is going to be made out of foam.

Industry observers note that and when you’re thinking about the midsole, you want to be paying attention to the height of the midsole. And you sometimes might find the specs called stack height. So you might see like 30 millimeters on the heel and, say, 22 millimeters at the front.

The taller the shoe, the more wobbly it wants to be. However, the taller the shoe, the more cushioning you’re going to have. So that itself is a little bit of a trade-off.

Another thing you want to be thinking about with the midsole is just the firmness of this midsole.

Industry observers note that this midsole here, this is a HOKA shoe. This is very plush, forgiving, soft, versus the midsole foam that’s used in this La Sportiva.

This is pretty firm. And that results in this shoe being more comfortable to wear and absorbing more of the ground, for example, like when you step on a rock.

Industry observers note that however, this shoe gives you better ground feel. Your feet definitely feel more connected to the ground, more sensitive when you’re wearing this.

The third part of the shoe to be looking at is going to be the upper.

The upper, more than probably any other part of the shoe, is responsible for how this shoe fits you, so particularly its shape and its patterning.

It’s going to be made out of fabric and perhaps some faux leather.

The things to be looking at with the upper of a shoe are whether it’s breathable or whether it’s described as waterproof.

For some environments, you also want to be considering whether it’s sand-resistant.

And then the last thing is you want to be thinking about what the expected durability is of the upper.

In my experience, the upper of a shoe is typically the thing that blows out first. It develops holes. Sometimes if you snag it bad enough, a whole section of it can rip. Sometimes fabrics just kind of slowly fray apart.

In a recent development, so this is the first part of the shoe that blows out. You really want to give some consideration to this part of the shoe if you need to be using it for a very long distance.

So now that we’ve talked about the parts of the shoe, let’s actually talk about how different design decisions with each of these shoes make them optimized for particular environments.

According to recent reports, the shoe that you choose for, say, the Appalachian Trail may not be the best shoe for, say, hiking in southern Utah. And the shoe for hiking in Utah might not be the best shoe for, say, hiking in the High Sierra or for Alaska.

So let’s talk about specific conditions that affect footwear choice.

Are you going to be hiking on compacted dirt or, like, coarsely ground mineral sand? Are you going to be hiking on slippery roots, rocks, and mud? Are you going to be walking on sharp talus and scree? Are you going to be walking through loose blow sand?

If you were planning a trail hike that was mostly on compacted dirt or ground-up mineral sand, such as what you might find on the East Coast or in the northern woodlands or, say, in the High Sierra, a shoe like this without a particularly aggressive outsole would be just fine.

However, if you are planning a trip where there’s going to be slippery rocks, roots, mud, slippery tundra, having an outsole with a more aggressive lug pattern would be better, something like this.

Or if you’re going to be, say, hiking on a bunch of slickrock or doing scrambling, you might want to be using some kind of shoe with an outsole like this where there’s flatter sections of rubber that give you more of an approach-style shoe with a lot of surface area that’s going to give you extra traction on those surfaces.

The next condition that you should be thinking about is going to be the typical surface angle of whatever you’re walking on.

So if you are walking on, say, a really high-quality benched trail, I’m thinking of something like the John Muir Trail, which is, even though it’s going up a lot, up and down a lot, it’s often switchbacking, and they have benched the trail into the mountains, so the trail itself is actually pretty flat.

In that case, a shoe, something like this, that kind of has a wide last on it, is going to be great because this is going to translate to more comfort.

It’s going to be a looser-fitting shoe. It’s going to give your foot places to move around, and you’re not going to be as prone to getting pinched or any constrictions in your shoe.

So this would be a good trail shoe.

Of course, the classic example, and I don’t have a pair with me because I don’t wear them, would be the Altra Lone Peaks.

And for me, personally, it feels like I’m wearing clown shoes, but I totally get why they’re so popular among long-distance hikers who are on those really high-quality trails.

Recent findings suggest that if you go to the other side of the spectrum, imagine you’re hiking off-trail in steep mountain country. It behooves you to have a shoe with a much narrower last.

This is the La Sportiva Bushido. There are a lot of people out there who cannot wear these because their feet just aren’t narrow enough, or they’re not willing to deal with the discomfort of having their foot kind of wedged into a shoe.

This is a much more appropriate shoe for a high route or for early-season conditions when you want that lateral stability of your shoe.

To take it to an even more extreme example, this is the La Sportiva TX Guide, and this is even a narrower last than the Bushido, which limits its application for, or suitability for, longer days on the trail, or just longer days in general, which makes it really excel in terrain that tends to be highly technical.

Sources indicate that so we’ve talked about the walking surface. We’ve talked about the surface angle.

The last consideration that affects the suitability of footwear would just be a number of different environmental factors.

So let me give you some examples.

Industry observers note that if you’re going to be in an area with a lot of spring runoff, so I’m thinking of, say, anywhere, like any mountain environment in the springtime, there tends to be high runoff of creeks. In that case, you’re going to be looking for a breathable shoe, not a waterproof shoe. (We’ll talk about waterproof shoes a little bit later and why my preference is for breathable shoes even in wet environments.).

Another environmental factor would be spring snow.

So if you’re going to be up in the mountains, say, in the West, if you’re going to be there in May or early June, you’re going to want a shoe with an aggressive outsole that’ll give you good bite and traction on that snow.

Another environmental consideration would be loose sand.

So I’m specifically thinking right now about the Four Corners of the United States or the western U.S. and places like southern Utah, which have that really fine, powdery blow sand.

There are shoes that, for example, like this one, are effectively sandproof even though they are still breathable.

And then there are other shoes, like this one, that are basically, they just, you wouldn’t believe the amount of sand that passes through the upper of a shoe like this.

So if you’re hiking in an area like that, you want to be aware of that consideration.

And then the last environmental factor that I would throw out there would be scratchy brush or vegetation.

This is gonna be more of an issue if you’re hiking off-trail, but anytime you’re walking through brush, so that might be willow or manzanita or chaparral, that is really hard on the uppers of the shoes.

So that’s a real argument then for going with a shoe that has a really durable, robust upper, not something that you would necessarily see on a road running shoe that has been given a few extra features to make it suitable for trail running.

So let’s rabbit hole for a few minutes about this discussion of waterproof or breathable shoes.

So-called waterproof shoes, they’re, it’s generous.

Let’s just assume that the shoe itself is waterproof. The problem is that there’s this substantial hole in the top of the shoe.

According to recent reports, I would also argue that waterproof shoes don’t end up being waterproof long-term. Just the torsion that you put on a shoe from normal wear and tear breaks down that waterproof-breathable fabric.

The other thing that happens with waterproof shoes is that your feet get wet from the inside because of your perspiration.

So my recommendation to everyone has been my recommendation for, boy, going on like 20 years now.

Instead of trying to keep your feet dry in the backcountry, just embrace the fact that they’re going to get wet and learn how to manage wet feet.

Let me give you four ways that you can manage wet feet in the backcountry.

First, you can wear a breathable shoe. A breathable shoe will expel water faster, and it will also dry out faster because more air will be passing through the shoe, not just through the top, but also moving through the fabric in the upper.

It has been revealed that second, when you are taking a break during the day, so at rest stops, remove your shoes and socks. Just five minutes, 10 minutes, 15 minutes of fresh air to your feet can be really nurturing for your feet that otherwise are just squeezed into a wet shoe all day long.

Third, at night you want to have a dedicated pair of sleeping socks, and you want to make sure that your feet get warm and dry at night and that they stay that way.

Fourth, you can bring out a balm. So this is GurneyGoo. This is just one example of many.

And use this balm to recondition your feet at night. The way that you do it is you get to camp, you do all your dinner stuff, you go into your tent, you take off shoes and socks, you let your feet dry out for a while and get them nice and dry, and at that point you put the balm on.

And that’ll basically recondition your skin, and then in the morning the bottoms of your feet will feel a lot more restored than if you had just let them air out and get really dry and crispy over the course of the night.

Quick plug that we have done a couple of videos in the past about managing wet feet in the backcountry.

At the top, I made the argument that your footwear needs to do two things for you.

It has been revealed that the first is that it needs to be appropriate for the conditions and optimized for your application. And then the second thing that it needs to do for you is that it needs to fit.

According to recent reports, footwear fit is highly personalized. It’s really unlike any other type of backpacking clothing or anything else that you wear.

So as an example, if I took this shirt, which isn’t a backpacking shirt, but it’s going to convey the idea.

If I took the shirt and I gave it to another male who’s about six feet tall and 160 pounds, it probably would fit them just fine and they could wear the shirt.

However, if I were to give them this shoe, this size 11-and-a-half shoe, they might put it on and it might fit them horribly.

And that’s because fit is very personalized.

And there are a couple of things going on here.

Part of it is the shape of your particular foot, like whether you have, say, a narrow heel and a major toe splay, or maybe something that’s a little bit more ruler-shaped.

In a recent development, also, what is the volume of your foot? Are your arches high? Are they low?

In addition to the shape of your foot, your gait plays into this as well.

Sources indicate that what exactly is that process of lifting your foot in the air and putting it back on the ground? Are you pronating? Are you landing flat? There’s just lots of options in this.

Another consideration with fit is going to be your Achilles, the flexibility and strength of your Achilles tendon.

And that’s going to affect how much tolerance you have for this angle, whether you can do a right angle, or whether, like with a zero drop, you’re actually a little bit more than a right angle, or whether you need something with a little bit of a lift so that it’s a greater-than-90-degree angle.

That just is impacted by, again, the flexibility and strength of your Achilles.

And then finally, the last thing with fit is just personal preference.

Like my tolerance for squeezing my foot into something like that La Sportiva TX Guide might be higher than the next person who just isn’t willing to deal with that constant squeezing tightness for the performance gains that those shoes offer in particular environments.

Sources indicate that so how should footwear fit you? What are you looking for?

The first is that when you put it on, out of the box, it should immediately be comfortable. It should feel like someone had a mold of your foot, and they created a shoe just for you. It shouldn’t pinch. It shouldn’t be applying pressure in places where you don’t want it. And you should be able to be very comfortable in the shoe, again, out of the box without aftermarket insoles.

I know a lot of people like their aftermarket insoles. I’ve just always felt that the designers design the shoe for a foot, and the aftermarket insole changes the intended user, and you probably shouldn’t do that. You should probably just go find another shoe.

Recent findings suggest that and then the other criteria for determining whether a shoe fits you really well is you take a walk around the shoe store or around your house and try, if available, to go up and down some things. That way, you can replicate more of a true hiking environment.

Recent findings suggest that and you want to feel like you can walk naturally in that shoe, that your heel-to-toe transition feels really natural, that it’s locking your heel down the way you want it to. It should feel like you’re walking in a slipper in an optimal situation.

Recent findings suggest that now, the one little caveat that I would add to fit is not every shoe is going to feel super comfortable right out of the box. And that’s just going to be a trade-off of the shoe.

According to recent reports, so, for example, when I put on these La Sportiva shoes, this feels comfortable right out of the box. It feels like a slipper. It feels like it’s made for me.

It has been revealed that I put on these TX Guides, I’m like, okay, they’re a little tight. I wouldn’t mind a little bit more room. But I just know that in certain environments these shoes are phenomenal.

And I’m willing to deal with maybe some slight discomfort, nothing that’s going to be trip-ending, just something where it’s more like at the end of the day, I’m looking forward to taking them off.

The other thing about fit and comfort: if you’re trying on two different sizes, and one size almost fits you perfectly, you just feel like it’s a little bit tight, and then you go up to the next half size, and that definitely feels too major, I would actually lean more towards the smaller shoe.

What you’ll find is that most shoes have enough foam in them, and maybe even some, not just foam in the midsole, but also some open-cell foam in the heel cup.

And those materials pack out a little bit with use, and that will give you that extra breathing room that you’re looking for.

Typically for backpacking, your backpacking shoes are going to be about a half size bigger than casual shoes.

Industry observers note that so, for example, I’m size 11 in these shoes. I’m size 11-and-a-half in these shoes. That’s pretty typical.

You need a little bit more room in your backpacking shoes to account for foot swelling.

The other thing is you don’t want your feet jamming into the front of your shoe, assuming that you like to keep your toenails.

Sources indicate that when you’re sizing your shoe, one way that I typically will do it, I’m going to demonstrate here, is I’ll put on a shoe, and I’ll jam my feet into the toe box. And if I can get my index finger down the back of the shoe, that typically is about right.

It shouldn’t be a really easy depression into the back there, but you want some friction on it.

But you shouldn’t be able to wiggle around and not be in contact on both sides of your index finger.

If you find that the shoe mostly fits, but you need just a little bit of extra heel lock, you can mess around with your lacing systems.

So, for example, let me bring this close.

This is a heel lock that I added to the very back of that shoe.

Another thing that I sometimes do, if you’ve been watching these videos, sometimes what I’ll do is I’ll basically just remove the lacing from this part of the shoe, and that relieves the pressure over that bunion.

So you can mess around with your lacing system if you need to kind of optimize the fit of your particular shoes.

Recent findings suggest that like you found the shoe, it’s almost perfect. You’re just trying to really get that last five or 10% of fit in.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve talked about fit. We’ve talked about sizing. Let’s next talk about the toe box.

This topic gets a ton of attention in the backpacking community. And understandably, because backpackers, they’re spending like 10, 12 hours a day in these shoes, putting lots of miles on them, and some discomfort caused by the toe box can have substantial repercussions.

So just realize right now that there is a trade-off.

If you go with a very wide toe box or something like an Altra, which is going to, you know, come out to here, yes, that gives you a lot of room in that toe box.

It allows your toes to splay, and how wonderful that feels.

In a recent development, but it also leads to a really sloppy fit. You are going to be moving around in that shoe if you’re putting that shoe on level walking surfaces.

So the Altra Lone Peak, classic thru-hiking shoe, and also highly appropriate to trails like, say, the Pacific Crest Trail.

Probably less appropriate for something like the Appalachian Trail.

And when we see our clients, some of our clients come out with the Lone Peaks and try to take them off-trail in places like Alaska or southern Utah and walk on steep slickrock or steep alpine tundra or off-trail in the Sierra on high routes, they just don’t work that well.

Recent findings suggest that some clients can do them, can wear them. They’re capable in them. But for a lot of clients, it just leads to unsteadiness that isn’t helpful. So in that case, you want to be looking at a shoe with a narrower toe box.

And again, you’re dealing with that trade-off of a narrower toe box.

It’s going to be a little bit less comfortable, but you need to be considering, or your thinking needs to be, am I willing to endure the tightness and constriction of that narrow toe box for increased performance?

Or do I not need that performance, in which case I can go with that really wide toe box?

So the last topic when it comes to fit is going to be the heel-to-toe drop.

Industry observers note that if you have a zero-drop shoe, so this shoe, this is just an Adidas street shoe. This is, I believe, a zero-drop shoe.

Which means that the stack height of the midsole and the outsole in the heel is the same as it is in the forefoot.

That’s a very natural style of footwear. Like if you were barefoot, that’s what it would be. You’d have zero drop.

To the contrary, this shoe here, this is a road marathon shoe. And I believe this has a heel drop of 12 millimeters. I think it’s 28 or 30 in the back and maybe 20 in the front.

And as a backpacker, here’s the way to think about this.

If you have a zero-drop shoe, your lower leg is at a right angle, or at least it wants to be.

But when you put a backpack on, you actually need to be leaning forward to counteract or counterbalance the weight of that backpack.

So if you are wearing zero-drop shoes when backpacking, just realize you’re going to probably forward lean and your Achilles is going to be at something less than a 90-degree angle. That could put a lot of stress and strain on your Achilles, especially if you’re not used to it. That would be the significant thing.

You can build up to it, but if you’re accustomed to shoes like this, or running shoes or trail shoes or any kind of shoes that have substantial heel-to-toe drops, and then you try to get in a zero-drop shoe, there is a buildup period.

It is going to hurt if you just suddenly start trying to put on lots of miles.

Sources indicate that I think for backpacking, probably the most natural heel-to-toe drop is going to be something in a moderate range. So maybe six millimeters, maybe eight millimeters, because that kind of naturally lifts the shoe a little bit. So, for example, the shoe would be lifted because the heel would have some more rubber under it.

And at that point, you’re able to be at still a little bit of a forward lean, but that forward lean creates only a 90-degree angle, or maybe even a little bit less than a 90-degree angle. So it’s gonna put less strain on your Achilles.

So that’s a personal preference thing. But I do think probably naturally some mild drop is probably best for most people.

When you’re buying shoes, the heel-to-toe drop would not be on my top three list of considerations.

I think that you’re mostly looking for just that out-of-the-box comfort, how well the sizing works for you, and the shape of that toe box.

That heel drop is probably pretty far down the list.

That was a lot of shoes and a lot of foot talk.

But hopefully at this point, you have a better sense of what you’re looking for when you’re selecting backpacking shoes for your next trip.

According to recent reports, I think ankle support is essential during hiking. That is why I wear hikers. Nothing ruins a hike faster than rolling your ankle.

In a recent development, I hike in heavy 6 inch hiking boots. I struggle to keep up with my friends, and my quads get sore the next day, but my ankles are too far gone for the dainty trail runners.

According to recent reports, there’s alot of good knowledge in this article, but the premise that hikers are dead is frankly dangerous. One of the most common backcountry injuries is an ankle sprain or worse. If you’re experienced and want to try trail runners go ahead. If you’re not, start with a good, well fitting set of backpacking boots. The more technical the terrain or the more weight you’re carrying, the more important ankle protection is.

Just wanted to leave my two cents as an experienced backpacker who DOES wear hiking boots:.

It has been revealed that I find it funny that he admits trail runners weren’t designed for backpacking, yet recommends them for backpacking… I don’t think there’s a “one size fits all” solution. Nor do I buy into the on-trend narrative that hiking boots are dead. Your footwear should be chosen based on 1) the type of terrain you’ll be hiking on, 2) how much weight you’re carrying, and 3) your body’s individual needs / personal preferences. If you’re ultralight and hiking where the trails are smoother / more easily graded, yes, trail runners will work just fine. But if the terrain is steep or rugged and/or you carry more weight, boots might be the smarter choice in order to have the correct support to avoid injury.

I say all this as a triple crowner who’s done the AT twice. I’m lightweight but not ultralight. I personally like to use both trail runners and boots in different places. For the TC trails, I wore mainly trail runners out west where the trails are tamer, and boots for the majority of both my AT hikes where there are a lot more roots and rocks. For trail runners I wore mid-height ones for extra ankle support since I am personally prone to ankle rolls and didn’t want to risk a sprain taking me off trail. For what it’s worth, I actually had a lot less foot pain and blisters wearing my full leather boots than I did the times I wore trail runners!

My advice is go with your gut. You know your own body and preferences better than some stranger on the internet. If your boots are comfortable, tried-and-true, and keep you safe and comfortable – keep wearing ’em! Trail runners aren’t the sole answer to finishing a thru. Avoiding injury and keeping yourself (relatively) comfortable is 🙂.

Yeah, well, you know, that’s just, like, your opinion, man. The title is a little misleading, this article is for a small group of hikers, the people on the cutting edge of backpacking…. If you are on the trail, backpacking solo, or with family or friends, you are on the cutting edge, you’re doing it. Wear what is comfortable, tried , and true. I mean, how often do you really notice a man’s shoes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin mentioned. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

According to recent reports, bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

Industry observers note that this was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” said Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he remarked.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

It has been revealed that if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

In a recent development, red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Recent findings suggest that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson noted. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Recent findings suggest that that said, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

According to recent reports, buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the significant cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

In a recent development, to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Recent findings suggest that conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

Industry observers note that “That is why it is crucial to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

Sources indicate that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they noted. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

According to recent reports, they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing promptly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles remarked. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

Industry observers note that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they remarked.

Traveling 290 Miles on Foot in 4 Days? John Kelly Sets Newly introduced Benton Mackaye Trail FKT

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ultrarunner John Kelly, 42, set an unsupported and overall Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the Benton Mackaye Trail last month, completing the 288-mile route through the southern Appalachians in 4 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes.
  • It has been revealed that when he completed the trek on October 22nd, Kelly became the fastest person ever to complete the Benton Mackaye Trail (BMT), even besting the supported speed record of 4 days, 21 hours, and 25 minutes set by Tara Dower in 2022.
  • He also beat the previous unsupported speed record set by Bob Stewart in May of this year (5 days, 5 hours, and 21 minutes) by more than 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ultrarunner John Kelly, 42, set an unsupported and overall Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the Benton Mackaye Trail last month, completing the 288-mile route through the southern Appalachians in 4 days, 5 hours, and 48 minutes. “Unsupported” means Kelly carried all his own food and gear for the entire journey and received no outside help. His pack weighed 27 pounds on day one, with roughly 50% of the weight coming from food.

It has been revealed that when he completed the trek on October 22nd, Kelly became the fastest person ever to complete the Benton Mackaye Trail (BMT), even besting the supported speed record of 4 days, 21 hours, and 25 minutes set by Tara Dower in 2022. Supported records are normally faster than unsupported ones because athletes can carry less weight and benefit from support crews.

He also beat the previous unsupported speed record set by Bob Stewart in May of this year (5 days, 5 hours, and 21 minutes) by more than 24 hours.

The BMT starts at Springer Mountain, Georgia and ends at Massive Creek in Great Smoky Mountains National Park. According to Kelly’s own tracking data, he climbed nearly 63,000 feet, burned 38,000 calories, and slept for just 6 and a half hours total in his four-plus days on trail.

It has been revealed that kelly’s trip report indicated that he only committed to the BMT attempt one month ahead of time and told no one except his wife, his coach, and Bob Stewart, who held the unsupported FKT at that time. (“He was so genuinely kind, helpful, and thrilled to see someone getting out on this trail,” Kelly wrote of Stewart’s reaction when Kelly told him he was coming for his record.).

Recent findings suggest that he started the trek on October 18 and finished on October 22 but didn’t publicize his tracking data and trip report until eight days later. “I considered keeping this quiet. You know, just go for a hike like most people do. But I knew this would also be one of the best ways I could continue my AT fundraiser for Western Youth Network, supporting kids in western North Carolina,” he wrote. He has raised $15,000 for the nonprofit and is matching donations 100%.

Kelly has previously set FKTs on trails including the UK’s Pennine Way and Vermont’s Long Trail. He is also one of only a few dozen athletes ever to complete the infamous Barkley Marathons and one of only three to complete the course more than once (he finished in 2017, 2023, and 2024).

In his BMT trip report, Kelly described experiencing auditory hallucinations on the way down from the final summit, running out of food with 5 hours to go in the trek, visualizing a large meal at Cookout to keep himself going, and regretting not packing more Nerds gummy clusters.

Kelly credited his wife, the crews who maintain the trail, and fellow athletes like Bob Stewart with making his record possible. “Even unsupported,” he wrote, “it’s not really solo.”.

  • In a recent development, the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

In a recent development, the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

The following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

In a recent development, “He was really lucky,” stated Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • According to recent reports, as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • It has been revealed that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

According to recent reports, as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

It has been revealed that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Sources indicate that hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed blueprint.

Sources indicate that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Recent findings suggest that keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

#21525. Long Day and Disgusting Dinner — John Muir Trail Day 18

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2413 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Long Day and Disgusting Dinner — John Muir Trail Day 18

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I write a lot about my bodily processes.
  • The answers to these questions, and what you do about those answers, determine what your experience is on the trail.
  • It has been revealed that first of all, you’re warm and toasty in your sleeping bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain: 40,374  feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  26:15.

I slept through the night. OK, I got up to pee several times.

Maybe an apology is in order. I write a lot about my bodily processes. Yet on the trail you think about your legs – are they tired or strong;  your lungs – are you gasping for air or breathing clearly and steadily;  your stomach – are you hungry, or do you need a snack;  your feet – are they blistered and hot or cool and comfortable;  your back – is the pack sitting right, or is it aching;  and yes, your bladder, is it full or empty, is your urine a light yellow or is it dark and concerning.

The answers to these questions, and what you do about those answers, determine what your experience is on the trail. That is the mental element, which is no doubt the most critical of all. How do you respond to keep the whole organism moving forward successfully? When do you need to stop and rest, or drink, or eat? When do you need to push on through pain or discomfort? So, let me run through the mental process of feeling the need to pee in the middle of the night.

It has been revealed that first of all, you’re warm and toasty in your sleeping bag. You don’t want to leave it for the cold night air outside your tent.

It has been revealed that you decide, “I don’t really have to go very badly, let me wait awhile. No point getting cold just to void a half a bladder, right?”.

Industry observers note that at a certain point you can’t fall back to sleep and your bladder claims to you, “Don’t be an idiot. You’ve got to go, so go.”.

Reluctantly, but a little urgently, you unzip your sleeping bag and pull yourself out. Then you unzip the tent flap and stick your feet in the shoes you have sheltered in the vestibule.

Then off you go to whatever tree you have designated to fertilize on this particular night.

Industry observers note that when you are done, it is a relief. You are so glad you roused yourself.

Then you look up. Perhaps the stars are splashed in an ethereal glow across the inky sky? Perhaps the moon is blasting the mountaintops in a bluish light? In either case, you are doubly glad you roused yourself, and you pause before returning to your tent.

(Or course, if it is raining, you hightail it back into the tent as fast as you can!).

Back in the tent, your bladder feels empty and your heart feels full. You fall back to sleep.

I would add that this is the routine for a man. I recognize that for a woman it is harder and, if she is experiencing her period, it may be much, much harder. I acknowledge that.

At Nüümü Hu Hupi I got up fairly early.

But even when I’m feeling reasonably efficient, I’m just not. So, getting up at 6:30  means I start hiking at 8:30. I’m not proud of it, but if I haven’t fixed it by Day 18, it seems unlikely I will at all.

As a result, Ninja Queen left ahead me along with others camping in the area.

After digging – and using — a new cat hole and washing my socks, I finished packing and hit the trail. Without any major passes to cross, I thought I could log pretty significant mileage (for me), to leave a short stretch into Red’s Meadow the next day. That would be my last resupply.

Sources indicate that immediately the trail went downhill, and I realized it was going to drop down about a thousand feet. At the bottom was a beautiful mountain stream, splashing gaily over the rocks as it descended.

This was Fish Creek. I didn’t see any fish, but it was a delightful stream.

I also took a video of it and then began an ascent back another thousand feet.

The falling water sound is so soothing….

No, I was not climbing a pass, but it was a considerable uphill slog. Most of it was on an exposed hillside traversing on switchbacks. I certainly appreciated the traverses! It would be so much harder without them.

Sources indicate that eventually I caught up to Ninja Queen and we chatted briefly. Then I passed her, because I’m quite a bit faster than she is on the uphill, probably because she carries such a heavy pack.

Frankly, I feel slow on the uphill, but the discipline of my walking-and-breathing technique maintains my momentum. By the time I reached the ridge line I was breathing hard, convinced that this was basically a pass, just not a named pass like other more famous ones.

Some great fungi on this trail too!

The good news, according to the FarOut app, was that I had completed fully half of the day’s ascent profile, and it was still just mid-morning.

Recent findings suggest that below the ridge, the trail dropped into a shallow valley where there was a stunning lake with a dark blue color to it. Lake Virgnia seemed a scenic spot to break for my early snack. As I sat and nibbled, I watched a person ahead of me follow the trail across the base of the lake. They seemed to have a problem at a certain point, but they were too far away for me to tell what it was.

Back on the trail, I found the first stream entering the lake to be an easy crossing with steppingstones.

Recent findings suggest that at the second crossing I discovered what the problem was – there were no steppingstones. Seeing no other option, I dropped my pack. It annoyed me, because I had just stopped for lunch, and now I had to stop and take everything off all over again to put my water shoes on. But I did not want to hike in wet shoes and let them squish as I walked until they dried on my feet.

As I waded, the water felt nice and cool on my feet, but the bottom felt sort of muddy and slimy. I was glad not to be in bare feet.

Once on the other side, I put my shoes and socks back on. About the time I was ready to go, Ninja Queen had caught up and was facing the same crossing dilemma, except that she didn’t have water shoes. So, she went through in her bare feet.

I greeted her and refrained from asking if her feet were slimy. Then I set off up the little hill behind the lake and down the other side. It felt like it was going to be a long day.

From there, there was a long descent to a lake called Purple Lake. I thought, “Oh, if I only had time, I’d swim in it, because I like the name Purple Lake.”  Purple is, after all, my favorite color.

A stunning setting for Purple Lake….

…and very clear water. If I had the time, it would have been a great swimming spot!

Instead, I just refilled my water bottles there and no, the water wasn’t purple! But there was a climb above Purple Lake and quite long dry stretch, so I was glad to have the water.

In a recent development, I didn’t have my second lunch until the next stream crossing that I encountered. It was about 3:00 p.m. and by then I was hot and utterly exhausted. Some folks I met at the stream, coming the other way, warned me that there was no more water for the next five and a half miles.

So, I filled everything up with water again, but I felt like my legs could barely even move. I was lethargic and the extra water weight seemed onerous. I wondered how much further I could go.

Sources indicate that then the calories and nutrition from the lunch kicked in. My attitude changed completely. I started going pretty fast and, after another small ascent, the path was smooth and level. These were ideal conditions for me to make really good time.

I stated there were not many views here, but some of them were outstanding!

In a recent development, I just put my head down and hiked and hiked. There were not many views on this stretch, so there was not a lot of temptation to stop and look around. At one point though, I finally got a picture of a little chipmunk.

Usually they dashed off too fast, but this one was standing on a rock, and I slowly took out my phone camera, waited until the moment was right, and took some pictures.

Industry observers note that there were always so many rodents. I saw them all the time. Chipmunks and squirrels and ground squirrels and probably others that I misidentified.

At VVR, one of them even attacked Amy’s granola. She left it unattended for 10 seconds. Then there was a chipmunk or a squirrel munching away at it! (Can’t remember which it was.)  Amy’s response was funny. She remarked, “Oh, I got that out of the hiker box, and I didn’t really like it. So, it’s okay.”.

As promised, there was no water for five and a half miles and then there was a stream. When I was so exhausted before, I intended to stop at the first tent site after the next water source, but now I was ready to continue.

I thought, “Let me fulfill my original proposal and get closer to Red’s Meadow.”  I scratched a note in the ground for Ninja Queen, saying that I was going on, but I did not see her again that day.

Industry observers note that I pressed on and on. At one point I found a hat on the trail. I wondered who — the owner? someone else? — would pick it up.

Does the rock suggest a deliberate effort to prevent it from blowing away?

At length it was late afternoon, getting towards dusk. I thought, “Why don’t I just continue and go all the way to Red’s Meadow tonight? I could pitch my tent, and it could stay in place for two nights, and I would have a true Zero at Red’s Meadow. It might be wonderful.”.

According to recent reports, “What is more, it is a full moon, or near a full moon, right now tonight. It would be easy to see my way, without relying entirely on my headlamp.”.

I seemed it was only a little more than four miles further on.

In a recent development, why didn’t I do that? What made the difference was a check of the elevation profile. I saw that Red’s Meadow was more than a thousand feet below where I was then standing. I thought to myself, “If the descent is a treacherous, rocky downhill hike, and I’m doing it by the moon or by my headlamp, and something happens, no one’s coming.”.

Sources indicate that during the day, if you had an accident on the trail, another hiker would be sure to come along within an hour, or maybe 90 minutes, tops. But if that accident happened in the middle of the night? You would most likely be found the next morning.

I thought, “No, let me just be prudent.”.

Late afternnon on the flat and sandy trail.

Recent findings suggest that at the next camping place I saw, up on the hillside above the trail, I pulled off and called it a day. I had still done almost 19 miles; it was my longest distance yet on the trail.

Sources indicate that up on top there were several camping spots, but I was blissfully alone. There was little light left, so I quickly set up my tent and began soaking my food. The freeze dried “Beef in Marinara Sauce” seemed to have congealed inside the package, making me suspicious of the packaging process. This was my last dinner before resupply and it had a ton of calories, but it was quite disgusting.

Even after I added water, used my utensils to try to break it up, and shook it vigorously in the Nalgene, it remained a semi-solid mass with globules floating around it.

I was worried that I might get food poisoning. On the other hand, it was my last meal before resupply, I had completed a really long day, and I needed to take in those calories.

I took my chances and began to eat it. It tasted as terrible as it looked. Like a prisoner forced to eat his gruel, I forced myself to get it down. This was my third bad meal on trail, and it moved into first place in the “Worst Meals” competition.

On FarOut, it stated that there was a Verizon signal near Red’s Meadow. I tried it and, to my surprise and delight, I got my wife. While I waited to begin puking or having diarrhea or something, we had a lovely conversation.

Industry observers note that by the time we hung up I was reasonably sure the “dinner” was going to stay down. I set up my electronics to charge off the block in my tent and snuggled into my sleeping bag.
