#21523. Industry News: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1699 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1699 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • The journey has not gone according to blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

The journey has not gone according to blueprint. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

It has been revealed that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid prepares. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Recent findings suggest that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

In a recent development, roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

Sources indicate that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and strategy ahead.

In a recent development, the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line indicates the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

In a recent development, I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

In a recent development, safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

According to recent reports, the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

In a recent development, the huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

You have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

Recent findings suggest that there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

Recent findings suggest that I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

According to recent reports, university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Industry observers note that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

It has been revealed that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

#21520. Rocks, Ridges, and Roads

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1227 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Rocks, Ridges, and Roads

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I continue my trek through Pennsylvania by facing off with rocky vistas, but also smooth gravel roads.
  • Recent findings suggest that progress in Pennsylvania has been swift, the trail follows a relatively straight path across Kittatinny Ridge.
  • According to recent reports, today should be somewhat eventful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I continue my trek through Pennsylvania by facing off with rocky vistas, but also smooth gravel roads.

Recent findings suggest that progress in Pennsylvania has been swift, the trail follows a relatively straight path across Kittatinny Ridge. The rocks are always a threat to slow things down, but I haven’t found it hard to do 20-25 miles a day even with daylight dwindling as the year moves forward. It feels like my last proper week on the trail. After I finish hiking on Saturday I will have just two more days remaining before heading back to Maryland to attempt the 4 state challenge. First things first, I need to get through this week.

According to recent reports, today should be somewhat eventful. I am hoping to squeeze in 25 miles, I will be crossing through a section of especially difficult rocks known as the Knife’s Edge, passing the unique Eckville Shelter, and ending near a popular viewpoint called The Pinnacle. I did well getting to sleep at a reasonable hour last night, helping me to start southbound from the Bake Oven trailhead around 7:30AM after my morning chores. My first thoughts when I got on the trail: “I am going to love hiking this last bit tomorrow!”. The trail was more of a dirt ATV path, flat, troublesome rocks removed, I could hike flat out, which I now really appreciate after the rocky sections that look flat and easy on the map but are a nuisance.

The flat trail was good while it lasted, but after a mile or so it reverted back to the typical Pennsylvania ridge hiking – a narrow, twisting path with mostly small rocks that weren’t bothersome. But then you’d look ahead and see a sea of boulders and think “the trail can’t possibly be routed through that?” And yet, that is exactly where it goes. I must not be too bothered by the rocks because I only hesitated a little when I saw a sign reading “Bear Rock” pointing to an enormous pile of rocks before sighing deeply and making my way to the top. This was no easy climb, there are blue blazes but hikers can still find plenty of ways up, none of them particularly direct.

A few more miles down the trail I came to another rocky section, but this one wasn’t optional. The trail narrowed to effectively nothing, the trail was just to follow the steeply sloped rocks and find a way to the other side. There was a decent view of the valley to the south, though more of my focus was on staying upright. This section is known as the Knife’s Edge. I don’t imagine it compares to the more famous/infamous Knife’s Edge on Katahdin. Scooby, a thru-hiker I encountered earlier in the year seemed to agree based on her comment on FarOut which I am going to shamelessly steal for your entertainment. I apologize for any language readers may find offensive:.

Knife’s Edge my biffin’ boppy! The only Knife’s Edge I know is In THE GREAT NORTHERN MAINE BAXTER WILDERNESS. How dare this thin squirrely rock formation disparage the great Northern edge.

View from the AT near the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter.

Industry observers note that I swung through the Allentown Hiking Club Shelter to retrieve a package. In a case of déjà vu, Pebbles had become separated from her Z Seat. I am told that it is actually Greasetrap to blame this time around. With the package secured, I continued along the ridge, which made up the first 14 miles of today’s hike.

The ridge continues west, but soon is divided by the Little Schuylkill River, so the Appalachian Trail shifts south to cross the river in Port Clinton. I won’t get there today, instead the trail heads south through the town of Eckville. There is a unique shelter just off the trail. The property was acquired by the National Park Service and turned into a hiker hostel/shelter in cooperation with the Blue Mountain Eagle Climbing Club, which maintains the AT in the area. In addition, Mick Charowsky, spent decades serving as the shelter caretaker. The property has a flushing toilet and a solar shower. I figured it would be worth checking out and getting a bit of water for my journey. I took a few minutes to peruse the logbook, finding a handful of familiar names, and adding my own name to the historic register.

Come with me, seat pad, you are needed up the trail!

The Allentown Hiking Club Shelter.

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

Looking across the valley at The Pinnacle.

The trail out of Eckville was the best so far in Pennsylvania. It was mostly a graded gravel road. I didn’t mind the gradual climb which lasted almost the entire 5 miles to The Pinnacle. By this point I had decided I would try to camp nearby so I could catch the sunset/sunrise from the overlook. I’d be coming up a few miles short of the 25 I had in mind, but I had space in my next itinerary to scoop those up. I headed straight for the rocks with my pack on and took in the scene. The Pinnacle sits at the leading edge of a ridge that drops sharply down to the valley just ahead of the viewpoint. An abundance of rocks ensure clear views. The only hitch was that the sun would be setting at the exact opposite angle from the rocks, it was the one thing you could really see. I figured it would still be perfect for sunrise tomorrow and set about finding a flat spot. I found plenty, though there were far fewer that weren’t so overcome with rocks that they seemed like they might lead to ancient Rome. I thought I had a decent spot, no rocks were visible, but when it came time to drive my tent stakes it is became clear that I had merely found a spot with about an inch of soil on top of a lifetime supply of rocks. I wiggled the stakes down until they were just about firm enough to hold for the night.

Birds circling above The Pinnacle.

Late afternoon view from The Pinnacle.

Total: 21.8 miles, 48,183 steps.

I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am fresh to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (382 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • According to recent reports, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

According to recent reports, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

On the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

According to recent reports, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Recent findings suggest that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

#21514. This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (769 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

This Is Why Your Trail Cameras Aren’t Working Properly

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • You’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot.
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s a newly introduced camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

You’ve finally got your trail camera set up in the spot. Every day or two it sends you a photo of a giant old buck, and now all you’ve got to do is wait for the right wind to sneak in there and hunt him. And then, all of a sudden, the camera goes dead.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a newly introduced camera, the battery life seemed fine, cell reception was decent … What the hell? Welcome to the often frustrating world of modern trail camera use.

Industry observers note that I’ve been field testing and running trail cameras year-round for several years now and in my experience, there is no camera brand out there that’s immune to malfunctions and failures. But my experience pales in comparison to that of Rich Howell of Trail Cam Pro. Howell has been objectively testing and experimenting with trail cameras for more than 20 years.

I recently interviewed Howell on the Outdoor Life podcast and he shared several reasons why hunters see so many camera failures in the field. Some of it has to do with how we’re using the cameras, and some of it has to do with how the cams are made (which is usually pretty cheaply). Plus, Howell hints at where he thinks the future of trail cameras is headed, and it’s all about making a system that is more affordable and useful to hunters. It’s a conversation worth listening to ahead of the heart of hunting season.

In the meantime, here’s why our cameras often go down in the field, and what we can do to fix them.

Standard alkaline batteries often don’t have the required power to keep a trail camera running reliably, Howell says. If you’re getting fine daytime pictures, but blank, black images at night, it’s a good sign you have a battery issue as there’s not enough power for the camera to fire the flash. This can happen even when the camera is displaying decent battery life.

According to recent reports, more expensive lithium batteries can work well, but they too can have issues. Howell noticed that about 1 in 20 lithium batteries would go bad very swiftly, (like within days of use) and sometimes this was enough to prevent the camera from working.

Howell now suggests that hunters use rechargeable lithium batteries, which have proven to be more reliable. Having a pool of these batteries on rotation will help solve many trail camera power troubles.

Industry observers note that when hunters first jump into the cellular trail camera game, they often like to get their photos sent immediately. In the beginning it’s fun to get a notification and then have that instant gratification of seeing a deer photo.

But it’s usually more effective to have a cell camera batch send images every 12 hours or 24 hours. This is a key way to preserve battery life, and it’s also a more useful way to analyze trail camera data.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I like to have cameras send every 24 hours and then I review all the cameras everyday in the morning. Looking at all the cameras on the property at once helps me put together activity trends.

Howell states that solar panels definitely can help keep your camera powered, but they often have issues in the field. First, you want to make sure that they are facing south to capture as most sun as possible. This can be a challenge if you want your camera facing north. And second, squirrels have a tendency to chew through solar panel wires. If you’re setting up your camera and panel in the hardwoods, there’s a good chance a squirrel is going to get to it. In other words, solar panels can be a useful tool, but they’re not a silver bullet.

Read Next: Best Cellular Trail Cameras.

Industry observers note that if you’re using the stock camera strap, you’re just asking for trouble. The tag ends of these straps always seem to come loose (triggering the camera) and you’re never able to position the camera perfectly on the tree with them. Plus, other hunters can easily spot the strap, which is an important consideration if you’re hunting public land. Howell suggests using an adjustable tree mount to make sure you can position the camera exactly where it needs to go. You can find a wealth of  trail camera information on the Trail Cam Pro website and by subscribing to their newsletter.

#21512. Pennine Way Wrap-Up

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1721 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Pennine Way Wrap-Up

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although I only completed 120 miles of the Pennine Way’s 268 mile route, I learned so much.
  • In a recent development, compared to the major thru-hikes in the US, the Pennine Way sees only 1,500 to 3,500 thru-hikers each year.
  • Over the course of my journey, I crossed paths with others infrequently and briefly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although I only completed 120 miles of the Pennine Way’s 268 mile route, I learned so much. What went wrong; what went right? To finish up this blog, I thought I’d summarize my experiences and lessons learned for anyone else who might be considering this adventure.

In a recent development, compared to the major thru-hikes in the US, the Pennine Way sees only 1,500 to 3,500 thru-hikers each year. On the morning I started, there were only two other people leaving Edale: Owen (aka SST) and Michael.

Over the course of my journey, I crossed paths with others infrequently and briefly. Some days, I didn’t see another person except at the pub where I had breakfast or dinner. There is usually a village somewhere along the day’s route. However, there are some stretches at the beginning and the end where there is nothing for two or three days. The terrain feels vast and trackless. If you don’t enjoy time alone, bring someone with you.

Sources indicate that that being mentioned, the British people were universally friendly (except the Uber drivers). There were many times when I was saved by the kindness of strangers.

The trail is boggy and muddy in sections, rocky and treacherous in others. Total elevation gain is more than Mount Everest. The wind is incessant and can be powerful. Although the temperatures stayed between a mild mid-50s to mid-60s, the wind-chill kept me bundled up even on hard climbs.

Sources indicate that when the rain comes—and it will come—it can be anything from a light drizzle to a torrential downpour. It might be both within the same hour. Most of the trail provides no shelter, manmade or otherwise. Full rain gear is essential. A tent that can be pitched in exposed areas in rain and wind will make a big difference.

I trained for this adventure in inclement weather and on technical terrain with steep climbs. However, the weather was worse than I had experienced and this made the terrain more challenging. Mental toughness in the face of physical hardship is a must.

Sources indicate that I’m one of those travelers who tends to make minimal reservations and just goes where opportunity takes me. This did not work so well for me on the Pennine. The villages along the route are tiny and services are very limited. You might hike all day only to find that there is no place to stay. Campgrounds close due to weather. Inns in the smallest villages may have less than six rooms. Many pubs stop serving food after 6:00 pm. Shops may close by 5:00 or 5:30 pm, and don’t open again until 9:00 am.

Industry observers note that while the notion of wild camping is romantic, it was also more challenging than I thought. You have to be far enough away from farms and villages to remain unnoticed. However, many of the truly remote locations are on windy, barren hilltops or boggy moors. The mental toll of not knowing where I would end each day, especially when the weather was really bad, began to take a toll after a few days.

Sources indicate that in retrospect, I wish I had researched more camping options and committed to reaching those locations. Knowing that I was going to be some place I could depend on, even if it took a couple extra miles, would have helped me push through. I think that’s how Michael, and Graeme and Rachel succeeded. Michael did a lot of wild camping, but he always had a solid idea of where he would stop for the night.

It has been revealed that finding trail markers can be challenging. Markers can be hidden behind overgrown foliage, barely legible, or missing entirely due to wind and weather. If multiple trails share the same route, not all the pertinent trails are listed. Some areas across the moors are completely unmarked, the trail only revealed through the boot prints of earlier walkers. I used digital maps linked to GPS, a highly-recommended guidebook, and physical ordinance survey maps. At times, these three sources contradicted each other, and sometimes disagreed with the physical trail markers.

In a recent development, graeme told me that having a second person to spot the tiny “acorn” markers was a massive help. From my experience, I wandered off trail at least once every day. Every time I fell, it was because I was trudging across wild terrain trying to find my way back. I feel fortunate that I wasn’t injured sooner.

Sources indicate that the guidebook claimed that there is no reason to bring more than a 12 kilo (26 pound) pack. I think the book assumes you’re not camping. My pack was 30.3 pounds without food. With food, I think I was carrying around 34 pounds. With the wisdom of hindsight, I would have packed differently.

I wish I had spent the money to buy a lightweight pack in the 45 to 50 liter range, and a lighter sleeping bag, retaining the 20 degree rating. Together, my pack and sleeping bag came in at nearly 7 pounds, a big chunk of my base weight.

Sources indicate that my research indicated that if I packed 5 days of food, it would last me to the end of the trail. I should have scaled back my packed meals to 2 days. While accommodations can be hard to find in the villages, food is easier. The pubs and cafes are frequent enough, and generally close to campgrounds. “Honesty shops” (little kiosks of food and drink, paid on the honor system) and snack shops are a welcome treat and usually close to the trail. Hearty snacks like cheese, protein bars and trail mix are good enough when you’ve had either a full breakfast or dinner in a pub. While the villages don’t have grocery stores, the smaller towns always had at least a convenience store for resupply.

Between a lighter pack and sleeping bag, and less food, I could have easily shaved 5 pounds or more off my total weight. For me, 27 pounds total weight would be ideal.

In a recent development, regardless of how gloomy all of the above sounds, I truly enjoyed my time on the Pennine Way. In fact, I’m already making intends to try again! I see what went wrong and I’m more confident than ever that the next attempt will be successful.

For more inspiration, I love this video by Fussyphotos.

Round trip airfare from the US cost me around $1,200 about 2 months before departure. When I was doing my research, that same flight 6 months before departure was around $850. Book early.

Sources indicate that I’ve you’re traveling from the US, an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) is required to enter the UK. It’s good for one year and cost me about $28.

Train fares from London to Edale, booked 30 days in advance, came to $170. This required multiple transfers across different transit companies. If you buy your tickets through an app like the Avanti West Coast, all the required tickets are sold as a bundle. This app was a lifesaver once I was forced off-trail and had to navigate by train for the remainder of my trip.

It has been revealed that bus and train fares from Kirk Yetholm to Edinburgh came to $40. Bus routes are managed by each local area, so there aren’t any apps. However, Google maps was accurate on routes and times and always helped me navigate the bus system. There is no advance ticket purchase, but I was able to tap a card or digital wallet on every bus I rode. Even the smallest villages and most remote bus routes accepted electronic payment on the bus.

Pre-booking my hotels 6 months early would have also saved me a lot. The difference between prices 6 months early and 2 months early was about 40 percent. Keep in mind that changing exchange rates will affect prices.

Recent findings suggest that A cheap hotel in Manchester and close to the train station, cost me $115 per night. I went straight from Heathrow Airport to Manchester, avoiding an expensive stay in London.

A major chain hotel in Edinburgh, close to the airport, costs me $255 per night.

It has been revealed that on the Pennine, the average price I paid for a double room with a private bathroom was $160 per night. Single rooms with a shared bathroom were often available at 20 to 30 percent less. Double rooms with only 1 guest were offered at a discount over the same room with 2 guests. If you’re traveling solo, make sure to adjust your reservation criteria on the inn websites.

Campground fees were generally $13 per night, sometimes discounted for Pennine Way walkers. I’ve since learned that this price can be per person. I wasn’t aware of this since I was alone.

My original plan was to camp for two nights and sleep indoors every third night. If I had kept to that plan, I estimate the trip would have cost me about $4,168. This excludes gear and airfare. Booking six months in advance would have brought this number down.

Industry observers note that my actual costs were quite a bit higher since I spent the second half of my trip off-trail shuttling between various towns and cities. I had additional transportation costs, and higher average lodging and meal costs for the latter half.

For my next attempt at the Pennine, I’m making several changes:.

As challenging as it was, I can’t wait to return and try again. With a bit of luck and a lot more foreknowledge, I’m going to make it all the way to Scotland!

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (338 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • Sources indicate that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Sources indicate that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

Sources indicate that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He stated climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#21510. Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2598 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Hunting the ‘Old Ripper’ Was Almost More Adventure Than I Bargained For

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I had just come back from the service in 1954.
  • In a recent development, old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp.
  • In a recent development, old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I had just come back from the service in 1954. My wife was expecting our first baby, and I was running a general store on Highway 97 just outside of Bainbridge, Georgia. Hardly a day went by that someone didn’t come in and tell tales of Old Ripper.

In a recent development, old Ripper was a large black wild hog that lived in the nearby Fowltown Swamp. That hog tore up more fences, broke more gates, broke the backs of more female hogs and was chased by more hunters than any critter there has ever been in this country. Ripper had been shot by several people. My Daddy fired at him seven times with an M-1 carbine and believed he hit him, but the hog never fell. He had been hunted with dogs and he had killed plenty of dogs. There never was a hog hound that could hold him. The last time the boar was run with hounds, he killed two of the best hounds in the county with his slashing tusks, so no one else ever put their dogs on Old Ripper.

In a recent development, old Ripper got his name because there seemed to be absolutely nothing he couldn’t rip up or utterly destroy. Farmers around Bainbridge went to the hardware stores and bought brand-upcoming aluminum gates to put in the gaps he made in their fences. Within a week, the gates were often all bent and torn up where that crazy boar had stuck his nose under and bent them to get into a pasture or field. There was no hog wire or barbed wire fence that could keep Old Ripper out.

That boar was walking destruction. The farmers hated him not only for tearing up fences and gates, but even more because of what he did to their sows. Ripper would break into a pig parlor, tear up the pens and release all the sows. Then he would take them off for a stroll in the woods. Old Ripper weighed 438 pounds. So when he mounted some of the young sows, he broke their backs. Then the sows would have to be destroyed. The sows he did breed threw shoats that were as wild and crazy as he was. The piglets wouldn’t fatten and brought almost nothing at the market.

Everybody was out to get Old Ripper. My dad was accustomed to catching wild hogs. We used to catch them in the Fowltown Swamp, fatten them and sell them at the market. My daddy knew about trapping hogs. He built traps to catch Old Ripper. On two separate occasions Old Ripper did go into one of daddy’s traps, but he tore up the wooden stockades and broke out both times. My daddy wouldn’t stand for that, so daddy got a steel bear trap and set it for Ripper. When daddy went back the next day he found the giant tracks of Old Ripper and followed them to the trap. But instead of catching a renegade hog, he found the bear trap had been sprung by the substantial boar.

According to recent reports, one reason Old Ripper became a legend was his ability to outthink the farmers and the hunters in our area. He had been around humans so much that in many cases he just outthought folks instead of using brute force. The people around our place began to think Old Ripper might be a supernatural creature. He was a boar, but he was a smart boar. No dogs could hold him, no stockades could enclose him, no fence could stop him and no man had been able to kill him for seven years.

Recent findings suggest that other episodes added to the legend of Old Ripper. One of the meanest things Old Ripper ever did involved Mrs. Ella T. Hand’s daughter-in-law, who was five months pregnant. She was in her kitchen and heard a disturbance out among her sows. She went out to the pig parlor and saw Old Ripper trying to tear the planks off the posts where she had her sows penned up. She picked up a rock and threw it at the old boar to try and run him off. When he saw her, he turned, looked straight at her and charged. Only a few steps away was a giant red oak stump that stood about three feet off the ground. The lady climbed up on the stump and began to scream for her husband. All the while, Old Ripper was going around the stump, snorting and blowing. He attempted to rear up on that stump and get to her but she stayed just out of reach of his razor-sharp tusks. For an hour the hog circled the stump as the lady screamed for help. Finally her husband came home. When he saw what was happening, he grabbed his shotgun from over the fireplace and ran toward the hog. At less than 10 yards, he shot Old Ripper in the side of the head with birdshot. The hog merely shook his head, looked at the man and trotted off.

In a recent development, to say Old Ripper was hated by everybody in the community would be a vast understatement. Every man and boy dreamed of killing that old boar, and plenty of work was forgotten by the men who hunted him. All it took to organize a community hog hunt was for someone to report that they’d seen Old Ripper. Every man and boy within earshot would grab a gun and head for the swamp.

It has been revealed that I would have liked to have hunted Old Ripper, but I had mouths to feed. I didn’t have time to waste on that renegade boar. I had just bought a brand-newly introduced lever-action Marlin .30/30. I was proud of that gun and took it out behind the store to test it out. On that particular day, Mrs. Ella T. Hand happened to be sitting out in front of the store. Mrs. Hand was close to 80 years old. She always wore a sunbonnet, a long dress and about 90 percent of the time, she had a dip of snuff in her mouth. Mrs. Hand saw me kill a crow sitting in the field about 150 yards away with that rifle. I knew I’d made a lucky shot, but she didn’t. She told everyone for a month about how good I could shoot with that new .30/30.

“If that old wild hog comes back around my sows, I’m going to come and get you, Jack, and let you kill him with that new rifle,” she told me.

According to recent reports, well, about a month later, here comes Mrs. Ella T. in her 1949 pickup truck.

According to recent reports, “Jack, that old boar is up in my field with some sows he run off,” she told me. “Now I don’t expect you’ll have any better luck than anybody else who has tried to kill him, but I sure wish you’d bring that upcoming rifle up to the field and give it a try.”.

It has been revealed that I closed up my little country store and got into the front seat of that pickup truck with Mrs. Ella T. to try my hand at Old Ripper. I had five cartridges with copper-jacketed lead-headed bullets in my gun—the kind that open up but still go on through. There wasn’t any doubt in my mind that if I could hit that boar, the bullets would do the damage needed to put him down.

We drove to Mrs. Hand’s 40-acre peanut field, which backed up to the edge of Fowltown Swamp. I saw Old Ripper out in the middle of the field with four sows he had just broken out from their pen. The five pigs were all rooting in the peanuts. There was a hog wire fence around the field, with barbed wire on the top. The field, which was about 250 yards wide and about twice as long, was on a hillside. Old Ripper and the sows were up close to the top of the hill and I was down near the bottom. There was a dried-up creekbed that ran under the fence. From the tracks in the wash, I figured this was where Old Ripper and the sows had gotten into the field. The creekbed was only about two or three feet deep, but it was massive enough for me to crawl under the fence and still stay out of sight. I could lay down in the bottom of the wash, crawl along on my stomach and Old Ripper wouldn’t be able to see me.

Until that day, I had never seen Old Ripper. I had looked at fences he had torn up and I had seen mud on the sides of the trees where he had rubbed. I knew he was a big boar, but I never realized just how big. When I saw Old Ripper standing there in the sun, his black bristles gathered in the rays of light and made him look a deep royal blue. He was a magnificent animal standing about four feet high, and he completely dwarfed the sows following him.

I said to myself, “Doggone your hide, Old Ripper! I’m going to try and get a little closer to you.”.

Recent findings suggest that the wash meandered from the bottom of the slope where I was uphill to where Old Ripper was rooting in the peanut patch. Lying flat on my belly, I would crawl for 10 yards and then peep over the edge to see where Old Ripper was. Each time I looked, the old boar was about 10 yards farther from the place than he had been before. It was just like he had a sixth sense that warned him of danger. He kept the same distance away, about 230 yards from me, from the time I first saw him until I decided to shoot. After I had crawled 30 yards, Old Ripper and his band of runaway sows were within 10 yards of a thick broom sedge field. I knew that if he got into that field, I wouldn’t be able to see to shoot him.

Recent findings suggest that the wash was shallower and just barely kept me out of the boar’s view. The shot had to be over 200 yards. So I laid the rifle down on the lip of the wash, looked through the open sights and aimed at the top of Old Ripper’s shoulder. When I squeezed off the first shot, I saw the dust fly off the boar’s shoulder and heard the bullet make a dull thud when it hit him, but Old Ripper showed no sign of being wounded.

Then I stood up. Old Ripper reared up on his hind legs and bellowed like a wild bull. The hair on the back of my neck stood up. I had caught or killed more than 100 hogs out of that swamp, but I had never heard a hog make a sound like that.

When Old Ripper came down on his front feet, he was on a dead run, headed right down that hill. I knew that when he got to the bottom of the hill, he had business with me. I should have killed Old Ripper with that first shot, but he was far from dead. I didn’t panic. I knew that before the boar got to me, I would have time to fire four more of those .30/30 shells. I thought there was no way I wouldn’t kill him before he got to me. I had faced other wild hogs before.

With every shot, I believed I was pumping more lead into Old Ripper, but he never slowed. He still came on toward me. I took my time, aimed, squeezed, heard the report of the rifle, jacked another shell into the chamber and fired again. I knew I was hitting the boar, but he never missed a stride.

When Old Ripper was less than 50 yards away, I heard the hammer fall on an empty chamber. That was the loudest, most desperate sound I ever heard in my life.

Sources indicate that I looked around and saw one lone cherry tree with no limbs on it about 30 yards to my right, but my feet wouldn’t work. I knew I couldn’t stay where I was, but I couldn’t go anywhere else. Old Ripper just kept on coming. I finally threw that gun down and began to run. Then I saw Old Ripper, now 20 yards away, running on two crippled front legs. I knew then that I had a chance to outrun him, but just as that idea went through my mind, the substantial boar fell and rolled to a stop about 10 yards away from me. He never moved, he never grunted and he never made another sound.

Industry observers note that there was a slight breeze coming from that dead boar to me. Old Ripper’s odor was the strongest, rankest smell I ever have smelled. It was awful. I waited awhile to make sure Old Ripper was dead. Then I looked to see where my bullets had hit. The first had entered the shoulder. The second went through the hog’s loin and had gone into his stomach. Two other shots had hit his fore shoulders and entered the chest cavity. One bullet just flat-out missed.

Looking at Old Ripper, I was kind of sad that he was gone. Even if he was a renegade, he was a magnificent animal. There had never been a boar like him before that I ever heard tell of, and there never was another.

Sources indicate that mrs. Ella T.’s son James and her husband Ressie helped me load Old Ripper onto the pickup truck. We took the boar to Mr. Smoke Roger’s platform scales at Fayetteville, Georgia. The boar tipped the scales at 438 pounds. We struggled to reload the boar and then drove back to Bainbridge. Dr. Cooper, the veterinarian at that time, examined him. Below Ripper’s inch-thick hide was a sheath of gristle that extended from his huge shoulders to the middle of his back. This sheath had been Old Ripper’s armor and had turned the shotgun pellets and rifle bullets over the years. Dr. Cooper said the boar was between 8 and 10 years old and was probably a throwback to some of the European wild boars let loose in this country years before.

Read Next: I’ve Been Charged by Bears and Moose. Wild Hogs Are Much, Much Worse.

When my daddy saw that the boar filled up the bed of that pickup truck, he could hardly believe his eyes. He had wanted to be the one who killed Old Ripper, but since he didn’t, he was glad it was me.

In a recent development, “That ol’ hog has cost farmers in this area thousands of dollars and many good sows, as well as being responsible for a lot of little pigs that weren’t fit to sell,” my daddy noted. “I’m glad he’s gone.”.

Since then the old Fowltown Swamp where Old Ripper used to roam and where wild pigs lived and bred for hundreds of years has vanished. Old Ripper’s haunts are covered by Lake Seminole today, but I remember it like it was when that boar was less than 30 yards away on a dead run bringing hurt to me, and I heard the sound of the hammer on my .30/30 falling on an empty chamber.

This South Dakota Hunter Borrowed a Bow and Tagged a 197-Class Deer — His First Archery Buck

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (621 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It wasn’t the best conditions for bowhunting in central South Dakota on November 3rd.
  • But Colby Claussen had seen a huge buck the previous week out of a tree stand and decided to buy a ground blind and place it near the trail where the buck had walked.
  • Industry observers note that “I spotted him a week earlier from my stand at nearly 70 yards walking a trail along a field edge near a standing corn field,” Claussen tells Outdoor Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It wasn’t the best conditions for bowhunting in central South Dakota on November 3rd. It was misting and drizzling rain and the wind was blowing between 20 and 30 miles per hour.

But Colby Claussen had seen a huge buck the previous week out of a tree stand and decided to buy a ground blind and place it near the trail where the buck had walked.

Industry observers note that “I spotted him a week earlier from my stand at nearly 70 yards walking a trail along a field edge near a standing corn field,” Claussen tells Outdoor Life. “He was working scrapes. I decided to buy an enclosed blind and put it in the woods 30 yards off the trail he walked.”.

A week later he was in the blind hunting the buck he’d seen on trail cameras off and on for several years.

“I first saw him several years ago through binoculars while hunting,” Claussen states. “The buck was a good 10 pointer then and about 600 yards away – way too far to shoot.”.

After that the 20-year-old hunter got trail camera pictures of the buck and watched him grow over several years.

“This year I saw him from my treestand working scrapes, but he was too far for me to try a shot with the bow I’d borrowed from a friend,” claims Claussen, a just-graduated student who farms with his family. The giant buck would be his first ever taken with a bow.

By 1 p.m. on Nov. 3, Claussen was in his ground blind, protected from wind and rain. He spotted a couple small bucks and does that afternoon. Just 10 minutes before shooting light ended that day, he spotted the enormous whitetail he was after.

“He stepped out of the woods to work a scrape at 30 yards, but it was too thick to shoot, so I waited,” Claussen says. “The buck stayed on the trail and kept coming toward me until he got in an opening, broadside at 30 yards.”.

Recent findings suggest that claussen drew his bow and shot an arrow tipped with a G5 Megameat 3-blade expandable broadhead. It hit the buck perfectly behind its shoulders, driving through both lungs, clipping its heart, and exiting the massive deer.

It has been revealed that “I knew he was hit well, and he went to the treeline, walked in a small circle, and disappeared into the timber,” indicates Claussen, who owns Sodak Drone Application, an agricultural business. “I went to where he stood and found my arrow and plenty of blood.”.

Claussen waited 30 minutes before trailing the deer, then promptly found the buck just 60 yards from where he’d shot it.

He called family members who soon arrived and helped with field dressing and loading the estimated 300-pound buck into a pickup truck. Then they took it to a meat processor, with the buck’s cape and head delivered to a taxidermist.

Read Next: The Best Hunting Blinds of 2026, Tested and Reviewed.

According to recent reports, A taxidermist measured Claussen’s buck at 198 1/8 inches, and another skilled deer rack scorer came up with 197 7/8 inches. The non-typical rack has nine points on one side, six on the other, with an inside spread of 21.25 inches. Antler base circumferences are 5 3/8 inches. The buck’s estimated age is 5.5 to 6.5 years.

“A couple years ago I had photos of that buck with half a broken rack from fighting,” Claussen says. “I quit hunting him when he broke his rack. But another hunter that year missed him in rifle season.

“I’m sure glad that hunter missed, and I got another chance to take my buck of a lifetime.”.

#21504. Saying Goodbye to our Camino Tramily

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (748 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Saying Goodbye to our Camino Tramily

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (748 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the next morning, our entire tramily caught a bus from Finisterre back to Santiago de Compostela.
  • Our bus snaked around the coastal cliffs all the way to the town of Orro before finally heading inland.
  • Our driver was incredibly skilled at maneuvering the narrow, winding roads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the next morning, our entire tramily caught a bus from Finisterre back to Santiago de Compostela. Even though the drive was only about 60 miles, the journey took over three hours.

Our bus snaked around the coastal cliffs all the way to the town of Orro before finally heading inland. It felt like we stopped in almost every small town along the Galician coast!

Our driver was incredibly skilled at maneuvering the narrow, winding roads. Every so often, the bus would come to a sudden halt in the middle of the road because the passing lane was barely wide enough for a single vehicle.

According to recent reports, looking out the window, waves crashed far below us. At times, the sheer dropoff to the ocean sat right at the edge of the pavement, guarded only by a short stone wall. Depending on who you asked, the ride was either thrilling or terrifying—but I trusted our driver completely. (A few passengers, however, definitely suffered from carsickness along the way!).

Once we arrived at the bus station in Santiago, it was time to say our final goodbyes to the tramily.

While we knew we would deeply miss their company, everyone felt excited for the next chapter of the journey.

After we exchanged big tramily hugs, the very first thing Knockerz wanted to do was head straight to Burger King for a predictable meal. A lot of our dining on the trail—especially when ordering hamburgers—has been a gamble regarding what kind of meat you actually get!

With lunch out of the way, we kicked off the final leg of our Camino journey by heading south, traveling in the opposite direction of almost every other pilgrim on the trail.

Over the next two weeks, our itinerary includes a mix of several beautiful variants:.

In a recent development, because we don’t have enough time left to walk all the way into Porto, we strategy to hike as close as possible. From there, we will take a short bus ride into Porto for a rest day (a “zero”), before flying to Paris and back home to the States.

Sources indicate that heading south took some mental adjustment. Everyone we passed was walking toward Santiago, and all of the yellow shells and arrow blazes were oriented for northern northbound travel.

According to recent reports, as a result, we constantly had to check our maps and make course corrections whenever we missed a turn. This leg of the Camino will definitely require constant vigilance.

After climbing out of Santiago along a mix of paved roads, dirt paths, and tight alleyways, we promptly made it to our final destination for the day: Millandoiro.

Recent findings suggest that millandoiro is a modern, cozy town. Our hotel felt surprisingly upscale while still being very affordable compared to prices back home.

According to recent reports, we spent the evening exploring a large grocery store located inside a small local shopping mall. The atmosphere felt familiar—teenagers hanging out away from their parents, and young families strolling through the concourse.

Inside the grocery store, the sheer volume of options overwhelmed us. It made us realize how spoiled we are in the States with massive supermarkets! Ultimately, we picked up prepared meals, drinks, and snacks.

According to recent reports, best of all, the front of the store featured a dedicated kitchen area with tables, microwaves, and utensils—a feature that only a tired hiker can fully appreciate. We happily heated up our dinner, relaxed at a table, and returned to our hotel room to unwind for the night.

After decades of no backpacking an abrupt life incident forced me back into the woods for some shinrin-yoku where I ran into a NOBO tramily at Shuckstack Fire Tower. That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a latest attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

The forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

According to recent reports, this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” remarked Kondrashkin.

Industry observers note that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

Industry observers note that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

Are Tree Saddles Really Better Than Treestands for Hunting Whitetails?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Industry observers note that early in my bowhunting career, I set up a ladder stand on top of a ridge that had oaks and plenty of deer sign. On opening morning, I watched a deer parade go down a trail that was 20 yards out of range. I sat in that stand several more times and never had a deer come within bow range. If I had a mobile stand, I could have easily adjusted my hunting strategy to move closer to the active trail.

Mobile hunting for whitetails is all about making aggressive moves and constantly hunting fresh spots. Mobile hunters carry everything they need for a hunt so they can set up on the fresh sign and easily adapt to the conditions. That’s why they need lightweight and easy to use hunting platforms.

Recent findings suggest that that old faithful ladder stand just won’t cut it when you need to slide another 100 yards closer to a bedding area. A mobile setup is also great for public land where you can’t or don’t want to leave your stand. It’s also less expensive than buying multiple permanent stands.

There are three main choices for the mobile hunter: a climber, a hang-on stand, and a tree saddle. I’ve hunted from all three of these platforms in my search for the perfect mobile hunting set up. To help with this comparison, I also reached out to Aaron Warbritton, from The Hunting Public YouTube channel. He’s been at the tip of the spear of the mobile hunting trend and offers a wealth of experience. Together we’ll see how each platform stacks up against each other in five categories: weight, setup, huntability, comfort, and price.

It has been revealed that A heavy pack can feel fine for a few minutes, but when yards turn to miles, you feel every pound. For hunting deep in public land, a lightweight set up is a must. Weights will differ depending on the model of stand and climbing method. These weights will give you an idea of what you can expect a complete kit to weigh. Here’s how all three systems compared:.

Model: Tethrd Mantis Saddle and Predator platform.

Kit Includes: Saddle, tether, platform, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

Total Weight: 14.1 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

Model: Lone Wolf Alpha Hang-On.

Kit Includes: Stand, safety harness, lineman’s belt, and three climbing sticks.

In a recent development, total Weight: 23.9 pounds. *The three climbing sticks separately weigh 7.5 pounds.

Model: Summit Explorer SD Climber.

Kit Includes: Stand and safety harness.

It has been revealed that if weight is your primary concern then a saddle is the clear winner. You can even make the saddle lighter by using a lighter climbing system.

Weight isn’t only a factor when carrying a stand, it also matters for setting it up. This is especially true when hanging a saddle platform or hang-on stand. When you climb to the height you want to hunt, you have to hold the stand or platform in one hand while tightening the stand’s straps with the other. A light platform for a saddle, like the Predator platform (3.3 pounds), is much easier to hang then the heavier base of a hang-on stand (12.2 pounds).

“I would say that now 90 percent of my hunts are with a saddle and a platform; just because it’s lighter, the footprint is smaller, and it’s faster for me to set up,” Warbritton says.

According to recent reports, with a saddle and a hang-on, you’ll need your choice of hang-on stand and a climbing method. I use the Lone Wolf Alpha stand and climbing sticks. The stand and sticks were designed to pack neatly together making it a very convenient and easy to use system. You can climb the tree and hang your stand in one trip with practice and some paracord. I’m pretty slow and careful when climbing and it usually takes me 15 to 20 minutes to climb and get set. The hang-on is fast, but the saddle is slightly faster and easier for me to set up.

According to recent reports, A climber is attached to the tree before you climb and doesn’t require climbing sticks. There’s also no platform to hang once you reach hunting height. You can scale a tree fairly rapidly with one, and it’s a less technical climb than a saddle or platform. However, that speed comes at the cost of versatility. Climbers need a straight, limbless tree, which isn’t always available. I much prefer the versatility of other platforms that allow me to climb almost any tree. If you live in an area that has a lot of trees suitable for a climber, then these negatives might not be such a significant deal.

The size of a climber is another negative. “I haven’t hunted out of climbers a ton, but I’ve hunted out of them enough to know I don’t want to use them. Their footprint is so major that when you’re packing them in, the stand gets tangled on stuff,” Warbritton claims.

It has been revealed that another reason to move away from climbers is the noise they make when climbing. It’s discouraging to put a lot of effort slipping into your spot, but then make a scraping noise as you ascend into position. This is especially true when hunting close to bedded deer.

It has been revealed that by comparison saddles and hang-ons are much stealthier to carry and set up. If you are proficient with either of them, you can be up a tree within earshot of a bedded buck without problem.

Proficiency doesn’t come overnight with any of these platforms, but tree saddles especially take time to learn. The saddle has a steeper learning curve because it’s so different than a traditional treestand. The first time you lean back into your saddle it might feel like leaning back on a rocking chair at the edge of a cliff. However, that uneasy feeling promptly fades and I personally feel much safer in my saddle than I ever felt in a hang-on or climbing treestand. That security comes from the fact that if you fall off your platform it is extremely easy to get back on because the tether is always pulled tight—making the drop almost unnoticeable.

Beyond the saddle’s learning curve, the hang-on and saddle are neck and neck when it comes to packing, setting up, and hunting out of them.

“They’re really close. They definitely have their differences. Whichever one that you decide to use, you need to practice with it. Whether you’re using climbing sticks or strap on steps, you need to practice packing, hanging, and then shooting out of them because they’re different,” Warbritton claims.

It has been revealed that when the rut kicks in and you basically live in a tree all weekend, a comfortable stand is a must. While all three mobile options are pretty comfortable, the standard treestand seat is hard to beat. Warbritton agrees with that preference.

“The only thing I like about a treestand is if I’m going to sit all day, I’d rather have a treestand,” he notes.

Tree saddles are comfortable, but a lot of the comfort in a saddle depends on your tether height because it controls the weight distribution. You’ll need to find a sweet spot that works for you and that takes some practice. I haven’t found that sweet spot for comfort just yet, but I do think that I’ll eventually get the saddle to be as comfortable as my treestands.

Read Next: The Best Tree Stands, Tested and Reviewed.

Like weight, the price will depend on the manufacturer and model. Just like our weight evaluation, we’ll compare the products I have personally owned and used.

A Tethrd mantis tree saddle, platform, lineman’s belt, tether, and a set of Lone Wolf climbing sticks will run you around $650. Without climbing sticks the system is about $500. If you want to add some accessories like Ropeman ascenders, pouches, and a recliner, you’ll be looking at spending around $900. It’s not a cheap investment, and you’ll have to decide if the above-stated benefits outweigh the cost.

Recent findings suggest that hang-ons and climbers are less expensive. A premium climber like the Summit Explorer SD and Hunter Safety System safety harness will run you around $450. A Lone Wolf Alpha hang-on, climbing sticks, Hunter Safety System safety harness, and lineman’s belt will set you back around $500. Again, prices will vary depending on what models, climbing methods, and add on accessories you choose.

Read Next: The Best Tree Saddles of 2026, Tested and Reviewed.

It has been revealed that warbritton and I both prefer tree saddles because they are lightweight, easy to pack, fast to set up, and make mobile hunting easier. Is it the best system for you? You’ll have to evaluate the features against your hunting needs to make that decision. The good thing is, all three systems will give you the ability to be a mobile hunter.

“I just think that either way you’re going to be hunting mobile and you’re going to have a lightweight setup that’s going to allow you to see more country, learn more stuff, and potentially kill more deer,” Warbritton says.

Breaking: Fresh Bear Canister Requirements on Georgia AT Spur Mass Migration of Bears to North Carolina

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to naturalists, most bears have chosen to “up and leave,” seeking more fruitful prospects in the less-regulated forests of North Carolina.
  • It has been revealed that map of Area Requiring Bear Canisters, via Appalachian Trail Conservancy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CHATTAHOOCHEE-OCONEE NATIONAL FOREST, GA – A recent order by the US Forest Service requiring bear-resistant canisters on the Appalachian Trail in Georgia has caused a dramatic stir in the bear populations local to the area.

According to naturalists, most bears have chosen to “up and leave,” seeking more fruitful prospects in the less-regulated forests of North Carolina. Witnesses have seen hundreds of bears traveling north along the Appalachian Trail corridor, preparing to hibernate closer to what will likely be next spring’s more plentiful food source.

It has been revealed that map of Area Requiring Bear Canisters, via Appalachian Trail Conservancy. https://appalachiantrail.org/news-stories/bear-canister-requirements-georgia/.

Human-bear interaction has been on the rise for decades in Georgia due to an increase in overnight hikers, with the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) referring to this inter-species mingling as “conflict” due to hikers “improperly storing food.”.

In contrast, delegates of the Georgian bear population describe these interactions as “mutually beneficial” and “charitable.”.

“For decades, we bears have benefitted from the abundant gifts generous thru-hikers have left us,” one bear told The PUD. “Every campsite is a bountiful buffet of ramen, Snickers bars, and Mountain House delicacies. The relationship is reciprocal too. Hikers feed us, and in return they get a cool story or sometimes a picture.”.

According to recent reports, given that many spring hikers in Georgia are new to backpacking, critters not only feast on poorly placed bear hangs and left-out trash, but often enjoy heartier items more seasoned thru-hikers would consider too heavy to carry, like fresh fruit or packaged meals. For the bears, it has been good eating.

But this cushy lifestyle is now at risk. The official order was signed by the USFS Chattahoochee-Oconee Forest Supervisor in Gainesville on November 6 and will go into effect January 1, 2027. According to the legal document, “All persons camping overnight must possess and use a bear-resistant canister for the storage of all food, food containers, garbage, and toiletries.”.

For many bears, this spells disaster.

Black bears migrate northbound out of Georgia. Photos by Diego Delso, Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Edited with Photoshop.

According to recent reports, following this upcoming policy announcement, hundreds of bears have begun their northern migration to North Carolina, choosing to hibernate closer to next spring’s food source. Wildlife biologists are describing this mass exodus as the greatest bear relocation event since post-glacial habitat shifts across North America and Europe in the late Ice Age.

Recent findings suggest that the exact route to North Carolina can differ for each bear, but many are opting to travel on the Appalachian Trail, given its mostly wooded and well-marked trajectory. Ironically, many bears have imitated the hikers that have caused their migration, creating detailed hike plans with similar mileage to their human counterparts. Sadly for some, the long days of walking have even resulted in a form of Hiker Hunger, which biologists agree is not ideal for a creature that will soon be hibernating.

Industry observers note that for most traveling bears, the journey does not end at the Georgia-North Carolina border, as the region already has a healthy bear population. Some Georgia bears have traveled as far as the Nantahala Outdoor Center. Staff at the NOC Outfitters promptly locked their doors and watched safely through the windows as the upcoming arrivals crossed the bridge to scrounge for leftovers at the Big Wesser Riverside Pub.

The newly introduced settlers are optimistic that the area will support their growing numbers this coming spring, counting on AT thru-hikers to immediately ditch their bear canisters and forgo any type of bear-proof food storage the second they leave Georgia.

While most bears have joined the trek north, some remain in Georgia, banking on some thru-hikers improperly closing their canisters or simply ignoring the latest guidelines altogether.

For those few bears staying, the reality of a changing food source is not overlooked. One holdout remarked that she knows it will be different, but she is willing to give it a try:.

“We hope the newly introduced backpackers will be carrying so much that they can’t fit it all in their canisters.”.

One particularly old bear has been the most vocal about remaining in Georgia. A long-time critic of the US Forest Service and a self-identified “Li-bear-tarian,” the elder Ursid calls the latest guidelines “a blatant act of government overreach.”.

“I’ve lived here my whole bear life and I’m not going anywhere,” the senior creature told The PUD through graying hackles. “I don’t need those Gainesville statists telling me, or any hiker, for that matter, what we do with our food. This is a free forest, ain’t it?”.

As a closing remark, the Li-bear-tarian added, “You don’t live in the backwoods of Georgia if you can’t live the backwoods lifestyle.”.
